item.title: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research
item.description: 270 points, 210 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (planned-obsolescence.org)

→ HN comments  ·  270 points  ·  210 comments

Top #1 — plaidfuji:

As somebody who does ML research, LLMs certainly make ML research faster. Maybe even 10x in some cases, as the author suggests.

But that’s just the parts of ML research that take place within your compute environment, namely experiments on model architecture, training strategy, UI/UX, etc. The algorithms and software.

Just because that part of research is progressively accelerated does not imply that we’re on a collision course with world-ending “superintelligence”. It just means that you’ll get to the best possible model of your data faster. And even when your data is the entire corpus of textual knowledge, there is a limit to the utility that provides.

It just means that software engineering, data analysis, and other computational tasks will be less of a bottleneck in the overall progress of the world (which, by the way, is great, and extremely valuable).

I don’t think it’s a stretch to say that we’ll have reached max LLM capability within a couple of years (what the author refers to as “super intelligence”). But it is a huge logical leap to say this:

> If we go through this feedback loop, I expect that the AI systems that come out the other side will be able to very quickly develop novel weapons and very easily overpower human civilization in a conflict.

First of all, the weapons necessary to overpower human civilization exist. They aren’t used as such due to geopolitics and humans’ basic survival instinct. Second, developing novel weapons requires physical tests, which are decidedly not accelerated by LLMs.

AI is a tool wielded by humans. If we’re wiped out by AI, it will be at the direction of a human. But we’ve made it pretty far with some pretty unstable humans in command of planet-killer weapons. I’m not overly concerned.

↳ reply 1 — Borealid:

I think there is something missed in how you're thinking about this problem.

Let's imagine that everything you say is 100% correct. LLMs can't access materials for developing weapons without weapons tests conducted at their behest, and humans choose not to - of their own volition - use world-ending weapons.

Let's also imagine for the purpose of conversation that one of the things that can be gotten at an extremely high skill level through increased intelligence is the power of persuasion.

A "superintelligence" persuades humans to perform weapons tests and then to give it the ability to use the weapon.

I think everything you've said is reasonable except the bit where you think step one of an "AI" exterminating humanity wouldn't look like a human doing it. In my opinion, the most likely vector for disaster is a human being who is "guided" by a computer model to do something unfortunate, not the model doing so directly.

↳↳ reply — Forlien:

What makes you think that persuasion isn't capped at some lower level than world-ending? There's a lot of incentive for ads to be as persuasive as possible, but they are so far from ending the world that it'd be science fiction for an ad to be that effective.

If you're just talking about convincing a few individuals to do experiments, then there are plenty of people who fall for scams everyday.

↳ reply 2 — joe_the_user:

There are a couple different questions

1) Does AI just guide developers to speed up the pretty much the same data-train-test model that we've had? Or does it inspire new, better algorithms that inspire further, better algorithms until you have superintelligence able to run on the hardware of today. The first option doesn't to promise exponential increases whereas the second one seems to. Notably, neither the statistics nor the anecdotes we read here point to the second option.

2) Is super-intelligence something that - in control of people or out of control of people - poses a threat to humanity? That's a huge question but it seems like something deserving thought today. Still, everything indicates the things will unleashed without very consideration despite this, given current momentum. So, IDK, get ready.

↳ reply 3 — kragen:

I think you lack imagination, but I'm not going to post ideas here for novel weapons that would render the humans' existing defenses and deterrence strategies ineffective.

It's worth pointing out that the humans do not have planet-killer weapons, not even biosphere-killing weapons. They could destroy civilization, but not the planet or even the species. You can make straightforward calculations showing that we already know how to build such weapons, but we haven't.

As for tools, alcohol, tobacco, fentanyl, pornography, monotheism, warfare, gambling, and money itself are "tools wielded by humans", but they still seem to get into a lot of trouble where it seems like the humans are the ones being "wielded" by the tool. And neither monotheism nor gambling is smart enough to write a compiler for me, much less choose persuasive tactics according to my personality type. A lot of humans' basic survival instinct seems to fail or even work backwards in the presence of these "tools".

Top #2 — chr15m:

Every dot in these graphs is composed of multiple benchmarks smooshed together.

Benchmarks are by definition a curated set of things that can be measured and evaluated.

Things that can be measured and evaluated can be (expensively) trained on.

The progress we are observing comes from figuring out how to measure and evaluate particular aspects of intelligence, and then expensively training on feedback loops made of those exact measurements, and synthesized data representing further measurements (literally benchmaxing).

What is not shown in these graphs are the set of things that intelligence can do, which are difficult, expensive or impossible to measure and evaluate.

That set of things is much larger than the set of benchmarks represented in the graph.

Therefore the post is misleading in the sense that the "superintelligence" being targeted is "jagged" to use Karpathy's term, and we infact already have jagged superintelligence (calculators, compilers, Bayesian spam classifiers, etc.)

We are witnessing a profound explosion of much more jagged superintelligence, restricted to the exact domains that can be (expensively) RL'ed on.

↳ reply 1 — reasonableklout:

This isn't really comforting to me for 2 reasons:

1. A key insight of foundation models is that capabilities are correlated. For example, training on code improved general reasoning capabilities: https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16298

2. A profound capabilities explosion in easily measured domains will still feel very different to today. Like, the moment we come up with a systematic, objective way to verify a task, we become obsolete at it?

↳↳ reply — novok:

IMO I think a partial root of why AI writing is so bad is because it's written like code. Like if you really dive into how it constructs things after iterations and ask it to analyze it , without it saying it's like code or without you saying anything about code, you'll notice coding like iterations.

↳ reply 2 — azan_:

Apart from physical world interactions which is obviously lacking, which domains lag behind and do not improve then?

Top #3 — nsilvestri:

AI is accelerating my work...work which only exists because of AI.

If I had to do my individual tasks without AI, I would be slower. But if I take a step back, I'm really not changing the world any faster than I was before.

↳ reply 1 — jack_pp:

I think where LLMs truly shine is personal greenfield projects, maybe start a side project

↳↳ reply — LeFantome:

Completely agree. LLMs are amazing for side projects.

The other place they are amazing is in working with legacy code bases. I mean, the kind the dev team always wants to throw away. First, even if you do want to throw it away, you can first find out what it does and realize it does more than you think it does. You can also create integrations to more modern components which can be used to extend it. You can also create a pretty decent test suite if you do not have one. And, once the behaviour has good test coverage, you can re-write it into something more modern. You can even completely change the architecture while ensuring compatible external behaviour. Remember, this is all in place of “throw it away and start over from scratch, only to discover that the scope is much larger than expected”.

↳↳↳ reply — simonask:

You could already do all of that. Like, none of that is infeasible to achieve on a scale of weeks in most cases.

It’ll still take weeks with AI in the picture, but for some reason management is more willing to plan it when they also have the additional token bills to pay.

↳ reply 2 — bhelkey:

> work which only exists because of AI

Could you elaborate? What work are you doing which only exists because of AI?

item.title: A Jev that can ask Opus for help gives Opus accuracy at 4x lower cost
item.description: 425 points, 96 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (hightouch.com)

→ HN comments  ·  425 points  ·  96 comments

Top #1 — muddi900:

If you are looking at huge categorizing and parsing work, using a local decision model and passing it to Haiku or Luna can really lower your token cost.

Top #2 — xlayn:

If you use Qwen3.8 27B to manage, to orchestrate, do do shallow research, and then make it ask claude you will notice that Qwen can get out of Haiku, Sonnet and Opus almost as good answers... I was researching how good the model asnswers where, I can't get to work with anything but Fable, but Qwen can get good work from any of them. My theory is that if you make Qwen understand you, Qwen can elaborate as much as needed to get any of those models get good results, because it's filling in details. So using Qwen to direct claude also get's you amazing results way way cheaper...

Update: let me elaborate more, I read the HN entry about the team of 5 Qwens being close to fable quality... so I embarked to add to my harness (https://github.com/alainnothere/privibe because we all have one right?) and once I had added the orchestrate tool I had to now measure somehow it it's able to improve quality, so I claude and then Qwen to run a experiment to call my harness passing the model to use and ask them to do something, 3 rounds I think and see what quality came out of it... and as per the grading... qwen and claude agreed that the quality of the response comming out the harness using the orchestrate was VERY CLOSE, with opus and fable providing more "in my opinion you should" which matches my experience on why they are better.

One more update: I can't get copilot models to work decently, it may be my way of working... but I can get Qwen to follow what I try to do... if Qwen get's me he can then fire copilot cli and get amazing results by using copilot... bonus points seems like copilot cli is cheaper with the AIC (cost of the requests) so you can make the copilot subscription longer

↳ reply 1 — drkleiner:

I do the opposite of this, use Qwen3.8-27B as subagents, Opus 5.5 as orchestrator and planner, never implementer, and it cuts my token usage significantly. So it is using Claude to direct Qwen. Never thought of the other way around, will give this a try soon as possible.

↳↳ reply — beefsack:

This is how I do it too. I run three levels:

  * Orchestrator: Opus 5.5
  * Feature lead: GPT 6.1 Sol
  * Worker: Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor
As long as you have an appropriate project and sandbox for Muse Spark it's the real secret sauce for my setup and it's dirt cheap on OpenCode Go.

GPT 6.1 Sol is surprisingly efficient too, I've been impressed with it.

My orchestration skill setup is https://github.com/beefsack/processed-beef/

↳ reply 2 — koolba:

> My theory is that if you make Qwen understand you, Qwen can elaborate as much as needed to get any of those models get good results, because it's filling in details.

How is this different than just telling the model you’re using to fill in the gaps itself?

If you’re not manually reviewing the intermediate hop, how does that add to the “understanding you”?

Top #3 — vouwfietsman:

Everyone is discussing the tech, but you do realize that they made mapping data to real people easier using AI? This is essentially AI-assisted privacy violation, 4 times cheaper.

People, please try to understand what you are building. Don't just build it as asked!

item.title: Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2
item.description: 211 points, 104 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (pwn.ai)

→ HN comments  ·  211 points  ·  104 comments

Top #1 — scoodah:

I really wish they would have expanded on this paragraph in their article further:

> The configuration used here had no jailer. Firecracker's production containment includes dropping privileges and restricting the process through namespaces and seccomp. A deployment using those controls requires a separate assessment of the privileges and resources available after compromising its VMM.

If I'm understanding all of this correctly, a properly jailed and configured firecracker instance would greatly reduce the blast radius of this escape, and I feel as though it would have been good for them to explain what jailing and dropping privileges would do to help. I'd hope most production firecracker deployments would be doing this already.

Not saying that this is any less severe and the root issue is not specific to Firecracker, but to a flaw in the kernel's network code -- they just used an insecure firecracker configuration to demonstrate it. However, I feel like some are taking this as a flaw with firecracker when its not. This is an issue in the kernel networking stack.

↳ reply 1 — tptacek:

That's a good catch. Yes, since they've only proven this up to the jailer boundary, you'd need a second and relatively powerful LPE vulnerability to get real host control out of this.

↳↳ reply — rvz:

Thanks to frontier reasoning agents, Linux is completely riddled in ways you can discover 900+ LPE vulnerabilities. [0]

Another wave of vulnerabilities like this are yet to be discovered in Linux. We are just seeing how weak C and C++ based OSes and kernels are when put under hundreds of AI agents.

[0] https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/

↳↳↳ reply — rockskon:

And how many of these vulns are in code for legacy hardware or filesystem support that in no way reflects threats against modern Linux installs? I wager the overwhelming majority of them.

↳ reply 2 — vluft:

yup, the other firecracker escape recently (https://www.coinspect.com/blog/firecracker-escape/) popped the jailer via io_uring (tl;dr firecracker was filtering syscalls appropriately with seccomp, and was filtering the uring _they_ initiated, so attacker just got them to pop a new unfiltered uring, which is rather nice).

↳ reply 3 — amluto:

Nope. The exploit compromises the host kernel. The researchers built an unconventional exploit chain in which they used the host kernel compromise to compromise the host firecracker userspace code, but I see no fundamental reason they couldn't have compromised something else in the host kernel.

Top #2 — lrvick:

I am more convinced by the day that the Nova Microhypervisor approach is correct.

Do virtualization with a tiny formally verified microkernel and have complex kernels like Linux run underneath instead of letting a huge, complex, and brittle linux kernel and vm ecosystem control the hypervisor layer.

https://hypervisor.org/

↳ reply 1 — eddythompson80:

How is this different from Xen? It's the same approach as Xen or Hyper-V where the hypervisor is its own component, then you boot into a virtualized Dom0 or Root Partition (in Xen and Hyper-V terminology respectively) that can manage the hypervisor underneath it.

This is different from KVM where your hypervisor runs in your Dom0/Root Partition.

↳↳ reply — markasoftware:

Xen had a generic guest to host vulnerability disclosed in the last few days: https://codeant.ai/security-research/xenbleed-a-grant-copy-c...

↳↳↳ reply — zobzu:

having worked with AWS, xen had a lot of very bad vulns over its lifetime as well.

there's no magic.

↳ reply 2 — tptacek:

I don't know much of anything about Nova but since the late 1990s this has also been the pitch for L4; there are several mature L4's.

Top #3 — zX41ZdbW:

I have a demo service that entirely relies on Firecracker VMs: ClickBench playground, https://benchmark.clickhouse.com/playground/

It hosts hundreds of database engines - many of them have vulnerabilities, and some of them, like Pandas, are basically open RCEs regardless.

We can PoC the Firecracker VM Escape on that service.

↳ reply — gavinray:

  > "run SQL against 110+ databases"
This is one of the most useful web tools I've ever seen.

I work on connectors for datasources (mostly DB's. Being able to quickly test things like sorting behavior and how the same function can be emulated across DB's would have made my life so much easier.

item.title: We know 15k websites are infected. how do we tell them?
item.description: 150 points, 130 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (scotthelme.co.uk)

→ HN comments  ·  150 points  ·  130 comments

Top #1 — baby_souffle:

Report each domain to the major browser vendors so they can update their list of suspicious sites?

I believe the default configuration for suspected spam and phishing and other malicious sites is that the user gets a red warning page that they have to click through first. Website owner would either get notifications from users or notice the drop off in traffic?

↳ reply 1 — Aachen:

I run a website where people can upload files. Not everyone uploads nice files. Every time someone downloads such a file from my site with their antivirus enabled, it's now my problem to discover which fifteen block lists the whole domain has newly been put on. People don't treat big tech this way; you don't think "oh, there's malware on Github, let me just report github.com as a suspicious website that nobody should be able to visit anymore"

The correct answer is probably the abuse contact shown in the WHOIS data. That's programmatically accessible and thus scales

↳↳ reply — JdeBP:

Let me offer the wisdom of the BBS Era, which had the same problem of people uploading bad files to small, oftentimes non-commercial, nodes: Scan files on upload.

Running anti-virus scanners immediately on uploaded files was a widespread practice in the BBS Era, adopted in response to the same kind of abuse. FTP sites did it, too. There was usually a delay for (run on a schedule) virus scanning between uploading to one of the shareware FTP sites and the file getting out of the upload directory and into the download areas.

The headlined article isn't really about hosting user-uploaded files, though. In no sensible system do user-uploaded files go straight into the site's own published JavaScript. The headlined situation is not analogous either to you or to BBSes, involving script hyperlinks to defunct third parties in one form of the problem, so what to do when it comes bad uploads from users is really going off on a tangent from Scott Helme's actual question.

↳ reply 2 — phyzome:

Yeah, this is probably the right answer. Immediately protects users, and website owners would quickly find out as well. :-)

Primary obligation is to the users, not the owners of websites that got themselves infected.

↳ reply 3 — bugfix:

Why not try to warn the owners first? Taking the site off of those lists is a pain.

Top #2 — Guestmodinfo:

Make a website, name it 15579infected.com and name everywebsite. Most of the website owners would soon wise up by word of mouth and visit your website and most probably contact you and you tell them what vulnerability each one has so they can rectify. You can charge them for your service.

↳ reply 1 — Jolter:

Charging them to detail the infection to them risks coming off as extortion to less savvy site owners. You might get a significant portion who would report you to the police rather than talk to you.

Just give them the deets.

↳ reply 2 — henearkr:

This is the right move. Contrary to what the other comment says, this is not "name and shame". Instead, this is a database, useful to check for website owners to see if their site is listed inside.

This would be an idea very similar to haveibeenpwned.com, which is immensely helpful.

Top #3 — theamk:

Work to add them to Google Safe Browsing blocklist (Why are they not on the list anyway? Surely Google will be interested in their technique)

Google, Facebook, Bing, other large platforms will get those websites blocked. Their traffic falls almost to zero. Then:

either web admin notices and fixes website

or people stop visiting yhem

either way, no more infected people, win for everyone.

↳ reply — Aachen:

> Then: \n\n either web admin notices and fixes website \n\n or people stop visiting them

Okay so let's say this is your site. You notice that Firefox gives a warning, you find the issue, remove the malicious dependency and roll out the new version. Now what? Who do you talk to to get unblocked?

I run a site that's on blocklists. There's no coming off of them once you're there (described elsewhere in this thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50398014). These mechanisms are useful for sites that are unmaintained, but I'd not wish it upon admins that immediately respond to vulnerability or abuse reports

I can understand that most people are not aware of this though, just a bit frustrating to see the call for nuking it altogether. It's not what you'd do if one of these 15000 sites was Onedrive: you'd realise the solution is talking to Microsoft. Only when they don't fix their infection would it make sense to take their site offline

↳↳ reply — theamk:

Most of the people report different experiences. I like this blog post, it also directly answers who does one need to talk to to get website unblocked:

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47183953

and another one, this was restored in a few hours:

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45538760

Now I am not saying it's a good thing there are so many blocklists, but there are sites who got onto them and then came back. I guess you are required to actually fix stuff, you can't just change nothing in your website and expect to be unblocked.

item.title: Devvm.dev: One VM for every project
item.description: 146 points, 57 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (devvm.dev)

→ HN comments  ·  146 points  ·  57 comments

Top #1 — photonios:

I keep seeing projects like this pop up and they never nail it.

I need isolation, but I also need to give my agents secure access to internal package registries, logs, internal infra, designs, emulators, browsers, docs etc. At a large company, work can span dozens of repositories. And on top of that, I need dozens of these.

I built this at work. Engineers use krunkit VMs with proper memory ballooning, GPU acceleration. Retina RDP, credential injecting proxy for etc.

This seems like a fun toy for single project development, but nothing close to what you need as an engineer in a corporate environment.

↳ reply — toyg:

I think this sort of thing can still be useful to smaller shops. I have a hobby project in this vein, and I know it will never make it big, but it's still a fun hamster wheel.

Top #2 — mnahkies:

Damn, I've been building something very similar the past few weeks - haven't quite gotten to a public release yet.

Mines based on libvirt and uses cloud-init for creating the images, with shared golden images across projects.

Skimming your docs it wasn't totally clear to me if your images are built per project, or COW from shared toolchains.

Looks like you have a few features in there that I might take some inspiration from though, eg the proxying stuff.

Funny how many of us are trying to solve the same problem at the moment.

↳ reply 1 — mnahkies:

One thing I'm struggling with at the moment which I may as well ask here.

Many of my projects use pnpm, which ideally uses hard links from a shared store of dependencies.

One of my goals is to reduce the disk overhead of VM based isolation, so I'd like a shared pnpm store across projects (and the same for maven, etc as well)

With https://virtio-fs.gitlab.io/ mounts, each mount inside the VM is a separate FS, and I can't hard link across them. I've tried playing around with ideas like bind mounting the directory structure from the host in a folder to have a single virtio-fs mount inside the VM - but the bind mounts still can't be hard linked across it seems.

I'm basically wondering if I'm missing something or just trying to do something that isn't possible.

All the host folders are on the same FS - but I don't want to organise the host system around the VM mounting needs, and I also don't want to mount extraneous directories into the VM (eg: simple solution could be just mount ~/projects but kinda self defeating)

(Fedora workstation host)

↳ reply 2 — vindex10:

add me as well. I learned about incus from HN ~a month ago, and was poking an idea of having a "development base image". The advantage compared to containers, is that you can hot-plug devices to the running instance: mounts, secrets, etc. incus also supports --vm and container mode with minimal difference in cli commands.

https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/

my main bottleneck was exactly in usability: how to make it least effort to spin up per use case and keep the set of operating scripts small - i didn't want to build an app for this, just shortcuts to use existing app.

Top #3 — jFriedensreich:

I see nothing this brings over smolvm machines. I did not use lima / krunkit outside colima but in colima it was just slow, had outdated devx and was unreliable compared to controlling every detail with an embedded vm library.

↳ reply 1 — LeBit:

I also moved to smolvm.

That project is underrated.

I have built my agent harness around smolvm and it has been working wonderfully.

I have seen a single bug up to now (iirc you cannot take a snapshot from a machine you rehydrate from a pack) but found a workaround.

I think the only thing I would love a solution for is the ability to bind credentials even when you use tailscale. You cannot right now because the traffic goes through the tailscale interface.

Anyway. smolvm is simply amazing.

↳ reply 2 — benatkin:

This is something that could run on top of smolvm, if the authors chose it, rather than Lima/QEMU. It both sets up virtual machines and what goes into them, letting you chooose toolchains and coding agents. smolvm doesn't provide dev tool setup within a vm, though it does point to images that already have toolchains and agents installed.

item.title: Anthropic IPO buyers see valuation as low as $1.1T
item.description: 270 points, 536 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (bloomberg.com)

→ HN comments  ·  270 points  ·  536 comments

Top #1 — UncleOxidant:

Sure, this is a small anecdotal datapoint, but since I've gotten Qwen3.8-Flash-Next running well on my Strix Halo box my Claude Pro subscription use has dropped off a cliff. I'm only at 18% of quota usage this week - this being Friday I would've been at 80% at least in the past. This is just an astonishingly good model that runs locally and quite well on my PC. I do not plan to renew my Claude Pro subscription when it comes up in a couple of months.

↳ reply 1 — sorenjan:

I really hope the future is local models, because the idea that all companies will need to buy tokens from a handfull of tech companies to run their businesses or make their products is awful.

↳↳ reply — beloch:

I've been ripped (on this site) for making this prediction. While the frontier (i.e. The toughest problems) will always push the limits of available computing power, what typical people do with AI won't always be on the frontier, nor will what appears on the frontier necessarily be lucrative. The frontier used to be playing Chess, Atari, and Go. These were challenging and really advanced AI, but they didn't make a lot of money. Now a phone can do these things.

You're an example of this process. You used to require a frontier model running on a data centre. Algorithms improved and, perhaps, your hardware as well, but your requirements didn't go up. Now you can do what you need to do with local hardware. You're one AI user who might not need to send money to Anthropic going forward unless you find a new frontier application that interests you.

This is why I'm a little bearish when it comes to the valuation of the AI giants. Yes, there are some extremely lucrative things on the frontier right now but, in the future, people may shift a lot of what they're doing now to local hardware while new things on the frontier may not produce the kind of profits that will pay back trillions in debt. AI companies have bet big on themselves being able to constantly and perpetually find new applications, and also that those new applications will make money.

↳↳↳ reply — shepherdjerred:

> but your requirements didn't go up.

I am definitely building more and more ambitious projects as models improve. Both personally and at work

↳ reply 2 — senko:

Interesting, I'm also comparing 3.8-flash-next (4-bit quant, llama for inference & pi as harness, on a 128gb strix halo machine) with opus 5.5 in claude code and while qwen is a good and fast model, it's nowhere near for coding, even haiku 5.5 feels better.

I could see it used as a sort of "sub-haiku" for easy stuff to leave more tokens for the bigger claude models, but I won't be cancelling my Claude sub any time soon.

↳ reply 3 — CharlieDigital:

I used Ollama with Qwen 3.8 27b on my MBP for a flight to try some experimentation and found that it was shockingly good at one of the more complex PDF processing tasks.

Like seat-of-the-pants good as Opus 5.5 but a bit slower and required just a bit more prompting to get what I wanted (which is fine for an app pipeline).

Top #2 — iamflimflam1:

The moat really is shallow to non-existent.

Both Anthropic and OpenAI are trying to build more tooling to try and lock companies into their ecosystems.

But I can’t help thinking that they are impacted by the very thing they have created.

You can now build your own enterprise tooling using the very models that they have created.

Top #3 — Bluestein:

I (all other issues aside) honestly think we have lost all sanity when the term "low" (in any fashion) can end up associated with 1.1 TRILLION.-

There is a serious, malignant, dangerous disarray somewhere in our callibration of value, of worth, of what things are worth. Something, many things, are wrong here.-

↳ reply — JohnMakin:

item.title: First steps in bare-metal programming using UEFI
item.description: 213 points, 40 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (kevinboone.me)

→ HN comments  ·  213 points  ·  40 comments

Top #1 — the_panopticon:

For "Get used to the lack of a C standard library" mentioned in https://kevinboone.me/efitest4.html there's always https://github.com/tianocore/edk2-libc.

And on "Be aware of the Windows-ness of EFI" commentary the resemblance to Windows coding style https://computernewb.com/~lily/files/Documents/NTDesignWorkb... is no accident. We leveraged this coding methodology as we evolved the original Intel Boot Initiative then EFI and then UEFI code and specification https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents...

↳ reply 1 — PerryStyle:

There's also https://libc.llvm.org/uefi/index.html, but not sure if it's still receiving updates.

↳ reply 2 — FuriouslyAdrift:

Be aware EDK II has a recent severe CVE to watch out for.

https://app.opencve.io/cve/CVE-2026-97631

↳ reply 3 — kragen:

I think "leveraged this coding methodology" is an unjustifiably positive way to describe the results of the process. I think "spread this disease" would be more accurate. UTF-16 strings, really? VFAT? PE32+ is maybe justifiable (I'd prefer ELF, but that's because it's more familiar, not because it's actually better), but VFAT? And even in 01998 it should have been apparent that UTF-16 was not a sane format for strings, much less in 02005 when the EFI → UEFI transition happened.

To me, UEFI is like "leveraging the waste disposal methodology" of dumping your toxic waste in a lake. Yes, it's more convenient for you, but it does lasting damage and causes years of suffering for millions of people; and eventually somebody else has to clean up your mess, at far greater cost than if you'd just done something sensible to begin with.

I could probably say the same thing about X-Windows.

Top #2 — kevin_thibedeau:

> The linker won’t complain if your code calls functions that don’t exist – it will just mark them as external, expecting them to be provided by some other code. But they won’t be, and the program will just crash when it calls one of these missing functions.

You can verify no external symbols remain after linkage with: nm -D --undefined-only. This can be incorporated into a build script to verify the binary is valid.

Top #3 — JdeBP:

Rod Smith and the OSDev Wiki went here, sometimes word for word, years before:

* https://rodsbooks.com/efi-programming/

* https://wiki.osdev.org/GNU-EFI

Of course, they both assume GCC on Linux. Change either one of those, and it is a wholly different kettle of fish. Both NetBSD and FreeBSD, for examples, come with an EFI development environment in base, squirreled away in /usr/src/boot in the case of FreeBSD. They have to, because they need to be able to build their own EFI boot loaders. NetBSD targets more than Intel processor architectures for EFI, moreover. (NetBSD can boot via EFI on ARM CPUs, for instance.)

item.title: Rune: A native GPU-rendered Rust UI framework for macOS, Windows, Linux and web
item.description: 149 points, 105 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  149 points  ·  105 comments

Top #1 — nicoburns:

If you're interested in a GPU-rendered Rust UI framework, then maybe skip this vibe coded project, and check out some of following established projects:

  Rust-native GUI frameworks (by crates.io downloads):

   1. egui (30.3M total / 9.2M last 90 days)
      https://crates.io/crates/egui

   2. Iced (3.2M / 770k)
      https://crates.io/crates/iced

   3. Slint (2.4M / 955k)
      https://crates.io/crates/slint

   4. GPUI (447k / 255k)
      https://crates.io/crates/gpui

   5. Dioxus Native (181k / 26k)
      https://crates.io/crates/dioxus-native

   6. Freya (49k / 12k)
      https://crates.io/crates/freya

   7. Floem (45k / 15k)
      https://crates.io/crates/floem

   8. Vizia (7k / 700)
      https://crates.io/crates/vizia
List is hand-picked list, ordered by crates.io downloads. I had an LLM fetch the download counts and links. Webview based UI like Tauri and Dioxus Desktop are excluded. As are bindings to native toolkits and GTK.

↳ reply 1 — bryanlarsen:

IMO, the top GUI framework crates for Rust are windows or native-windows-gui, objc2 or icrate for MacOS and gtk4-rs for Linux only. Actually for MacOS / iOS I'd use uniffi to embed the rust core in a SwiftUI app.

In 2026 IMO it's much better to use an LLM to keep 3 separate native front ends in sync than it is to try and use any sort of cross platform UI.

↳↳ reply — tadfisher:

An advantage of this approach is that everyone's screen readers and other accessibility tools actually work with your app.

↳ reply 2 — auraham:

https://crates.io/crates/dioxus-native was released 3 months ago and does not have a link to GitHub, I do not think it can be considered as established project yet.

↳ reply 3 — amelius:

Slint is proprietary. Given that AI makes it so easy to spec out and build even entire GUI frameworks, why would you even go with proprietary anymore? And why doesn't the article showcase a full-fledged set of UI components?

Top #2 — mik3y:

Sort of a digression, but it's the first time I've seen something like this:

    > We don't take pull requests. Have your agent open
    > an issue describing the bug or idea, and our agents
    > usually turn it around fast.
Pretty interesting approach, compared to receiving a zillion potentially sloppy PRs. Open source in the age of LLMs.. ("agent source"?)

↳ reply 1 — kodablah:

I did the same for a vibecoded project [0] but I would never do this for a human-written project. Simply put, if most contributions are similarly vibecoded and/or they will be reviewed/treated as such, then how is a PR/review from an unaffiliated agent any better than one managed by the project curator. Of course that human curation still needs to occur.

This is a natural progression (only on these types of projects). We accepted contributions because it actually helped and they were difficult and time consuming. When that is no longer the case, contributions are a burden, the actual problem/idea is the real value, hence the request to open the issue.

0 - https://github.com/cretz/vitaslop

↳ reply 2 — teekert:

I had a Nix issue. Agents fixed it in 5 min.

Of course, one could conclude that another agents screwed up before, still was a good experience.

Top #3 — rgbrgb:

> Every app can run headless, so an agent can render to PNG, dump the element tree and drive it with scripted input.

This is cool. I hope SwiftUI / UIKit borrow this idea for native mac apps.

↳ reply 1 — viraptor:

You can do the same thing with swiftui. The surface you render to doesn't have to be visible at all. And the tree has nice introspection available.

↳ reply 2 — 0x457:

Headless part is neat, but agents can already drive apps and take screenshots. As a side note, I have agent driving android tv using wireless adb and hdmi capture card + mpv rpc, its fun to watch.

item.title: Ask HN: What in the world is taking Ubuntu so long?
item.description: 179 points, 114 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article

→ HN comments  ·  179 points  ·  114 comments

Top #1 — throw0101c:

As outlined in this weblog post:

* https://ubuntu.com/blog/fixes-available-in-proposed-pocket-f...

The fixes were in the "proposed" repo since October 26 (noble) and 28 (resolute):

* https://launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/linux

One could pull them down at any point in the last week. Yesterday afternoon they were still in "proposed", but I checked this morning (EST/UTC-5) and they there were in "updates". Some tracking of timeline of when the updates to the repos happened seems to be available at:

* https://ma.ttias.be/linux-cve-2026-98432-vulnerable-kernels/

The kernels goes through an QA testing processes, and per this September post, they're looking at shortening the timeframe for kernel updates:

* https://canonical.com/blog/accelerating-delivery-of-cve-fixe...

↳ reply — gwbas1c:

> The kernels goes through an QA testing processes, and per this September post, they're looking at shortening the timeframe for kernel updates:

Looks like they aren't flexible enough to get a 4-line fix out the door when they need to.

These situations need a CEO or other high up to pull some people into a room, and basically say, "this needs to be released by EOD."

↳↳ reply — throw0101c:

> Looks like they aren't flexible enough to get a 4-line fix out the door when they need to.

Perhaps because Ubuntu, like most distros, release new kernels that include fixes and updates for more than one issue:

* https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2026:93413

* https://launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/linux/6.8.0-149.149

* https://www.suse.com/support/update/announcement/2026/suse-s...

* https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/DSA-6568-1

↳↳↳ reply — cassianoleal:

Perhaps that's the problem? Surely they use a version control system that allows them to branch off of older commit for these kinds of urgent patches.

Top #2 — imjonse:

Has there been a documented exploit of this CVE on Ubuntu or on the other distros before they were patched?

↳ reply 1 — talon8635:

Here’s the real answer. It’s not as scary as the original reporters made it out to be.

↳ reply 2 — arto:

See here: https://x.com/mattiasgeniar/status/2118040483154755627

Top #3 — atestu:

Seems like a good time to ask: what do people use, if not ubuntu, on a web server? Like for example for a rails app, on EC2... asking for a friend (who is me).

↳ reply 1 — kccqzy:

In the age of AI, there are only more and more security vulnerabilities to be discovered, and backporting all of them to outdated kernels will be nigh impossible. I’d not rather make such security patches dependent on the timeliness of backports especially if it is done by a distro rather than upstream. I suggest you use a rolling distro rather than anything with LTS kernels. The CVE in the original post CVE-2026-98432 is fixed since 7.3. If a distro doesn’t offer kernel 7.3.1 today, rule it out. (7.3.3 is also out today.)

In general I find distros using old kernels annoying because Linus treats compatibility seriously and “don’t break use space” has been a mantra for many years. On desktops in particular, GPU driver improvements like https://www.phoronix.com/news/Linux-7.3-DRM make it super worthwhile.

As for exactly which distro, it matters less than you think. I use openSUSE Tumbleweed but plenty of my friends prefer Arch.

↳↳ reply — SahAssar:

That is a wild take, especially consider the GP asked for a server use-case. Do you just assume that all new versions should be taken as soon as possible for all packages?

There is a balance: too outdated is bad, too eager for new versions is bad. The tradeoff that LTS tries to take is older, proven versions but with relevant security fixes quickly.

↳ reply 2 — mad182:

I personally use Debian both on my servers and desktops, for the last 15 years or so.

item.title: University libraries are being swarmed by AI bots, putting public access at risk
item.description: 128 points, 58 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (cbc.ca)

→ HN comments  ·  128 points  ·  58 comments

Top #1 — Bender:

LLM bots are the easiest to spot. Rate limit them to 16kb/s and 1 request every 5 seconds. Give them a friendly multilingual WCAG status 429 page that says to slow down or status 444 and drop them into nftables ipsets if they continue to be aggressive. Ask your favorite LLM how to set this up. If your LLM gets session paused, ask Gemini or Grok. Tell it if you are behind a CDN. Enable logging of ssl curves, ciphers, etc... Show your LLM some examples from your access logs.

↳ reply 1 — eatonphil:

I get tens of thousands of IPs making 1 or 2 requests against pages on The Consensus (job search, code viewing, etc.). They're not super expensive pages. But I don't want to deal with the bot traffic (mostly because it messes up view counts I use to sell sponsorships). But then if I require an account (even a free one), valid readership is also going to drop with the new friction.

I could build something more complex to discover the patterns, or use Turnstile maybe. I'm not really sure at the moment.

↳↳ reply — EvanAnderson:

I mind a public access website for a government entity and this is exactly the pattern I see. US residential IPs make a couple of requests then never come back.

The bots may have layer 7 signatures that make them "easy" to block, but I'm dealing with COTS software with no ability to make changes to the stack. Even if I could by the time they're blocked the work is done and they're never coming back anyway.

I don't think I'm seeing the LLM bots in the scraping on this particular site. This site's data is highly sought-after by data brokers, legal services advertising, debt collectors, etc. I tend to think I'm seeing homespun scrapers. This site has been up for 20+ years and the scrapers seem to be well-adapted to using the HTML as an ad-hoc API for the data. The difference in the last few years has been the availability of vast numbers of residential proxies to mask the traffic.

↳ reply 2 — dmtroyer:

I think you overestimate many organizations ability to implement this type of rate-limiting.

Top #2 — blakesterz:

What I still don't understand is who is doing it? I assume it's not the big companies like OpenAI or Google or Anthropic, right? So there are a bunch of small things out there doing the scraping and then they sell it to the big places? Or are these just smaller AI models doing the scraping and using it for themselves? Is there an underground ecosystem where people buy and sell this stuff? I understand why it's valuable to the AI companies I'm curious about how all this work, the economics of it all.

↳ reply 1 — qingcharles:

Can't speak for everyone. I'm very gently scraping a lot of libraries for public domain periodical scans. The scans often exist nowhere else, or not in the same quality. Sometimes I find a certain library has perhaps the only known remaining intact copy of a periodical or a specific page.

The problem with the libraries is that all these scans are behind walls, so while the texts are public domain nobody can easily access them. I'm trying to liberate them and re-upload them outside the walls.

Until recently a lot of libraries would allow you to remotely sign up for a library card, but in the last 12 months almost all of them have reverted to having to bring ID in person to the library to validate your account, which puts the brakes on things.

↳↳ reply — sriacha:

I've been looking at historic newspapers recently, its bothersome and unfortunate that many (most?) are all behind newspapers.com (ancestry) paywall.

↳↳↳ reply — qingcharles:

Yeah, I'll be on ancestry.com and it says "We found this article about your great-grandfather!" and then you click it and it's newspapers.com and I have to close the tab.

What's the solution, though? All these newspapers won't scan themselves. I'm setting up a non-profit right now to deal with the magazines. The rights issues are both better and worse with magazines. "Better" in that most magazines have gone out of business and the rights are cheap. Worse in that most of them are orphans and the rights are very hard to track down.

↳ reply 2 — TazeTSchnitzel:

We're currently in the middle of an AI goldrush. There are probably hundreds of companies trying to do model pretraining. Anthropic and OpenAI and so on probably care about optics and implementing their crawlers properly. But there will be many firms few of us have heard of. I would guess some of them are Chinese, for example.

Top #3 — londons_explore:

Behind nearly every AI bot is some human who will see real benefit from scraping my site.

I just make sure all my pages are super lightweight to cache and serve from cloudflare and let the bots do what they like.

If I put something on the internet for all to see, I want bots to be able to see it too.

I've been on the other side of bot blocks - when I ask my LLM to buy me X and it comes back and says the only place it could buy from is some Bulgarian seller because everywhere else has anti-bot scripts, I make sure to give that Bulgarian site my business.

item.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production
item.description: 629 points, 1388 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (nbcnews.com)

→ HN comments  ·  629 points  ·  1388 comments

Top #1 — brightball:

After Helene knocked out power in parts of my area for a little over 14 days, I found out that a friend of ours used his cybertruck to power his house through the entire mess. He'd run the house on it for a couple of days, then drive the cybertruck over to a super charger station, recharge, then come home and plug the house back in.

The battery capacity on those things is equivalent to 9 Tesla Powerwall units or something close to it.

They may be ugly, but the emergency prepper in me always wanted one after hearing that story. Before, I always wanted to install powerwalls...but I never considered in an extended event being able to drive my powerwalls somewhere to recharge them.

↳ reply 1 — rurp:

This seems like an awfully niche case, no? How often does someone lose power at home for days, while also having a nearby and accessible charging station that stays functional the whole time? Most of the disasters I'm aware of people either get their power back in a short enough amount of time that they can use a normal generator for the gap, or things are bad and widespread enough that they aren't driving down the street to recharge their vehicle.

↳↳ reply — masklinn:

Also very important: the cybertruck is not the only vehicle capable of doing that (the keywords are V2H and V2L, V2H is the more convenient — the car just plugs into the mains and acts as a house battery — while V2L means you have to go and plug your stuff to the car's mains outputs directly)

> Most of the disasters I'm aware of people either get their power back in a short enough amount of time that they can use a normal generator for the gap

TBF an EV car has an absolutely massive battery relative to the electric consumption of a house, unless you're using resistive heating all around. Especially if you ration use.

↳↳↳ reply — jayknight:

Here's Alex from Technology Connections testing powering things in his house from his Hyundai Ioniq 5.

https://youtu.be/yO5fJ8z66Z8

↳ reply 2 — spaceywilly:

Another way to view this is that driving a cybertruck every day is quite wasteful (no different than driving a full size gas pickup every day). One recharge cycle in a cybertruck uses enough energy to power a typical home for 8 days, 130kWh. If you aren’t doing truck things with it, it’s better to drive a more efficient EV or hybrid car. It uses almost twice as much Wh per mile compared to a model Y.

I think this is why these EV trucks don’t do well (ford also cancelled the F150 lightning). For truck things, they aren’t particularly capable (you’d get less than 100 miles towing). For daily driving duty, a car or small suv is much more efficient. You can power your home during a storm from most EVs these days, you’d just have to top it up more often

↳ reply 3 — lrobinovitch:

This is now a feature of most new Tesla vehicles:

https://www.tesla.com/powershare/#vehicles

> Powershare is currently available for all Cybertruck vehicles, and all new Model 3 and Model Y2 vehicles ordered on October 1, 2026 or later.

item.description: 126 points, 82 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  126 points  ·  82 comments

Top #1 — sgt:

Had a look at their website [1]. Initial thoughts: this is a bit ridiculous, I can just build that myself. And in fact, I have done already.

Thoughts after about 3 minutes of browsing: OK, this actually makes sense and I see why people would pay for this. The value proposition is definitely there

[1] https://www.getunleash.io/

↳ reply 1 — ivarconr:

Thanks, "I could build that" → "oh, that's what the other 90% is" is pretty much how Unleash started for us too. What does your homegrown version do? Always interested in where people draw the line between building and adopting.

↳↳ reply — sgt:

Just basically various means of turning features on/off based on static rules. Settings mostly but occasionally user based or URL params.

Your platform has that and a ton of other things that would be useful for larger platforms, but it would be a pain to develop when you're already building a complicated roadmap.

↳ reply 2 — amelius:

Hmm, after 5 minutes of browsing I still don't get it.

↳ reply 3 — cfontes:

I pay for it for my team... it's expensive to be honest, but worth it IMHO. Building it would be a ok, supporting it a pain.

If you work on a small startup, not worth it... on a Big corp with a lot of bureaucracy? It's worth it I think.

We have tried self-hosting it, but it's always a pain to allocate people on infra to do it, so I gave up and started paying for it for my teams, and they love it.

Top #2 — 0x70dd:

Yesterday I saw that LaunchDarkly is a $3B company. How crazy is that?!

↳ reply 1 — notfried:

A million monthly active users, even free ones, would cost you ~$10K/month on LaunchDarkly. A million sounds like a lot, but "active" can mean one visit, even anonymous users. ~$120K/year for feature flags is a ridiculous line item.

These SaaS companies are only valued this much because they charge based on MAUs, not request-based. I prefer PostHog's model. 100M requests/month is ~$2K [*].

[*] I'm not affiliated with PostHog.

↳↳ reply — ivarconr:

On Unleash Cloud: 100M request per month on Unleash cloud would be $235 + 75$ per seat ($53 Million requests included).

↳ reply 2 — vouwfietsman:

Shoutout to ConfigCat, https://configcat.com/

Same features as all these big guys, EU hosted, and down-to-earth pricing. Even the free tier got me quite far.

I'm unaffiliated btw.

Top #3 — jonhohle:

Are most feature flag systems really just simple Boolean checks like this with no feedback loop? In 2009 Amazon’s equivalent supported multi-variate flags (run test with more than 2 options), a feedback loop for performance/attribution, and weighting. I don’t see any of that on the unleash home page, but also haven’t seen it in other feature config systems either.

↳ reply — hobofan:

What you are describing is usually part of analytics platforms (Mixpanel, etc.). A feature flag toggle only plays a small part in this (but it may also be used for a lot of other scenarios of how you may want to control feature flags).

Audience is decided by analytics tool -> Feature flag server maps audience to feature flag value -> Analytics tool tracks its events and includes feature flag value as attribute

↳↳ reply — jonhohle:

So if you want to slowly roll out a feature flag, you need to get a different app involved that can do everything the feature flag tool can do and a whole lot more? What’s the point of the feature flag tool?

Analytics is a much broader set of tooling. It can (and should) report similar things.

↳↳↳ reply — hobofan:

The point of the feature flag tool is to control feature flags. They are not just for A/B testing and slow rollouts, and most products are not on the scale of Amazon, where you need to have a feedback loop for the rollout. Of course there is always going to be some overlap between tools, where many analytics platform allow you to do the rudimentary version of this.

The main point of a FF system is that you have a runtime-controllable mapping from user attributes to feature flags, where a set of logic rules can dictate who is exposed to what feature. With most analytics-tool based rollouts, you would be able to only directly set an attribute and you then hard-wire that attribute to the feature toggle in app code, which gives you a lot less flexibility and always requires a engineer in the hot path when it comes to doing rollouts.

I'd like to use this moment to praise ING. I have an old tablet running quite modern LinageOS. The ROM is rooted and I use apps that require root accounts. Its almsot only purpose is banking. I don't have banking apps on my main phone.

I have ING app installed on the tablet, the only issues the bank has with it is I get more notifications wanting me to do online training on cyber security or being scammed. I get the same notification every few weeks that my device is rooted and it is "potentially more vulnerable", I can click "I understand" or "Learn more". No other issues, it's not blocking me from doing anything, not forcing any updates, doesn't limit any functionality of the app. Despite my salary is not paid to ING, ING is my main bank. ↳↳ reply — teekert:

↳ reply 2 — kioleanu:

In all fairness, you can’t normally do shit in the ING app without them warning you that you might be getting scammed, even on modern devices

Top #3 — stef25:

In Holland, GrapheneOS users are being targeted by police after "busting" a re-seller. The owners of the phones got raided without them being involved in any investigation. Just having the phone was enough to get a knock.

Supposedly the Dutch police had "cracked" their phones.

In Dutch https://archive.is/3wawb

↳ reply 1 — microtonal:

You fell for really shoddy reporting by AD/HLN:

According to our information, the reseller did not distribute official GrapheneOS. Using AI tools, he had built his own fork and added mobile device management (MDM) for remote administration. The result was a separate operating system that lacked, among other things, the security updates of the original project.

His signing keys for that system were probably compromised. Anyone holding those keys can build an update that the phones accept as genuine. Such an update was apparently installed on seized phones via ADB (Android Debug Bridge), an interface that requires a USB cable connection, and probably removed the screen lock. The phones could then be examined forensically. On our information, the authorities again needed the phone in their hands. On official GrapheneOS, the same approach would require the project's own signing keys.

https://www.joint-defense-team.com/post/grapheneos-cracked-p...

↳↳ reply — ledoge:

I don't think the attack can work as described here. One of the features that GrapheneOS lists is:

> Insider attack resistance for updates to the secure element (Owner user authentication required before updates are accepted)

From my understanding, this means that even if you do have the signing keys, you cannot install an update that would remove the need for knowing the screen lock to unlock the filesystem's encryption - as installing such an update requires entering the screen lock first.

↳↳↳ reply — buzer:

However if you have signing keys and access to the update delivery infra you could just publish the update and wait for it to get auto updated before starting to seize the phones.

↳ reply 2 — 3abiton:

This is the issue with being lenient on crime but also being liberal. You have to search for the "right" patterns to find your criminal. It happens that folks who care about privacy, and criminals, two distinct groups search and use the same set of technologies: wether it's grapheneOS, or others. I am also tired of people still looking suspicious at me for not having instagram, snap or tiktok or use whatsapp, it's like I dropped out of society, and that I use linux and use open source email clients/server, I use ublock origin advanced with blocking of scripts and 3rd party domains. Why privacy is an uphill daily battle.

item.title: Britain to make salary disclosure in job ads mandatory
item.description: 532 points, 414 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (reuters.com)

→ HN comments  ·  532 points  ·  414 comments

Top #1 — dotdi:

I will repost a comment I made here a while ago on a similar discussion. Salary non-disclosure is a dealbreaker for me since being through the situation described below:

A few years back I wanted to get out of the work situation I was in. I looked around, had some interviews, had some offers. None of the postings had salary ranges, as is common where I live.

My eyes, however, were set on a specific small company because I liked their product. The process was long and involved multiple meetings, a take-home problem, and stretched over 2 or so months. I was upfront about what my salary expectations were (wasn't looking for a raise, just a lateral move). They said we discuss salary when you meet the founders, i.e. the last step before getting hired, but they also didn't tell me that my range was way off.

Turns out I had played this 9 week game and turned down other offers just to be severely low-balled by them. Maybe they saw that I really wanted the position and thought they could get away with a low offer.

Obviously, I rejected their offer on the spot. I also promised myself to never, _ever_, be fooled like that again. We talk money before I invest any significant amount of time or I walk.

EDIT: fixed wording.

↳ reply 1 — cs02rm0:

I've done worse than that. I've taken the job on a lower salary, being told I'd get a promotion and pay rise in 6 months. That didn't happen. And then when it didn't happen at 18 months they dangled the carrot of a promotion up two levels. After a few weeks of not hearing about it I popped a resignation letter in the post one morning, went into the office and had an email to say the promotion had "gone away".

Then they went legal trying to prevent me working for a competitor.

I actually got what I needed from the role anyway, but it was a lesson to heed the red flags. I've not heeded that lesson a couple of times recently, just because the market seems to be toast, but it's not been worth it.

↳ reply 2 — DeusExMachina:

A friend that works as a manager told me that companies stretch the interview process on purpose so that at the end you will accept a lower offer that you normally would because you are exhausted by the process.

↳ reply 3 — kevin_thibedeau:

> small company

> Stretched over two months

These companies aren't Google. There is no valid reason why it should take so long to decide on candidates for a position. It is not necessary to have more than two interview sessions. I bail on any company that subjects people to this garbage.

Top #2 — aregue:

I have always felt that job ads should include salary information. The main reason is not to waste anyone's time. Often a narrow salary range or a clear link between requirements and salary are much more informative than a job description. I have experienced to apply to a job opening and go through one or more interviews only to find out that the company is actually hiring for a more junior position than the ad copy implied.

A second reason is to avoid discrimination. Applicants that feel disadvantaged, even if they are actually qualified, may hesitate to negotiate for a higher salary in the same way that a other applicants would. The consequence is that they start with a lower salary. This applies specially to women. Plenty of research shows that they are less likely to negotiate their salary.

Research[1] suggests that pay transparency leads to lower average salaries because employers avoid paying higher wages to any one employee to avoid costly negotiations with others. The effect is small, around 2%, and it disappears with increasing degree of unionization. In my opinion this is an acceptable price to pay to reduce pay inequality, which often is much more than 2%. It is also a good argument for joining a union.

[1] https://www.nber.org/papers/w28903

↳ reply 1 — arpinum:

When hiring I don't have a narrow range in mind, it can be 50% or more. I look at the individual and make a judgment call on their impact to the business. For software we don't have a widget factory where employees are easily substitutable.

I've tried the opposite, paid everyone the same. But there were clear differences in ability and more importantly outside options. It became a problem when it came to retention and the business didn't have the ability to overpay everyone to keep the top performers.

↳↳ reply — chaosharmonic:

You're describing levels. If your range is so wide the top of the range is double the bottom of the range, you're hiring at multiple levels, and you should just say that. You should also have more detailed descriptions that help you and candidates differentiate what those levels are.

More broadly than that -- it's not that you need to pay everyone the same, it's that you need clear structure around how your pay works.

An example that became a problem with one previous employer was that they kept saying "performance" was their only determining factor for pay, after it had come out that exactly one person on our team had been offered bonuses as a performance incentive.

It's not actually performance-based if you have different and better reward structures, or if you can't/won't explain why gaps exist.

↳↳↳ reply — arpinum:

It's mainly specialties, not just levels. Are you a graphic designer that can also build your designs for the web? Were you previously consulting for our largest customer? Do you speak Welsh for our important client in Pembroke? Did you previously work in tech stack X and want to get back to it, and could lead our effort into that market? I'll pay more for these even if they come in at the same grade. Pay is very subjective, it is a prediction about the value an employee can or does bring balanced against their next best option.

↳ reply 2 — lelanthran:

I've always asked, and then get the generic "for the ideal candidate we are prepared to go very high", which I tactfully point out as the BS it is - there is no role that has ever been advertised without a manager or director-level sign-off on the range.

I usually reply to the brush-off with "I only ask because the seniority level is reflected in the salary, not the role or the advertisement."

I say that because it is, in fact, true: the seniority/skill required for the role and duties/responsibilities dictates the pay, the bullet points in the advertisement and the role description is often completely divorced from the level of seniority or skill required in the actual role.

IOW "We're hiring a Senior dev" might have me respond "That's a Junior pay-bracket".

Top #3 — ellen364:

item.title: I struggle to believe that AI R&D is ingenious
item.description: 147 points, 143 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (lesswrong.com)

→ HN comments  ·  147 points  ·  143 comments

Top #1 — mangecoeur:

Llms are far from being ingenious or innovative. The main way they can surprise you today is pulling in information that’s new TO YOU - I impressed with the algorithms they pop out sometimes simply because never formally studied compsci. But when it treads on my home turf I find it very basic, and for bigger picture stuff like system architecture its terrible, by its nature it doesn’t have a “vision” of how the whole system fits together

↳ reply 1 — z3t4:

It's like reading a news paper, when it's about your field of expertise you find lots of errors, but when it's about something you don't know you take it at face value.

↳↳ reply — layer8:

The short name for that is Gell-Mann amnesia.

↳ reply 2 — manapause:

Strong agree. My 30 years of experience building computers and breaking them has made me better because I don’t trust my knowledge or myself as a first principle. If I didn’t have that and I could easily see myself in an alternate reality, coming in late to the game to leverage ai to build a car out of seatbelts; harnessing all the power of 1000 suns seeing that idea to fruition.

↳ reply 3 — BenoitP:

Strong agree, but with a major caveat: First since we humans don't have a memory the size of the internet, new TO YOU is extremely easy to find. And second: a lot of discoveries can be made by trying to match two different domains and generate new insights at the seams.

A lot of math theorems are discovered that way by humans btw: find a difficult problem in a domain, map it to another domain, apply existing theorems there, go back to the original domain. The only difference is an LLM would have to search for an interesting problem, but that can be done by brute-forcing search at the seams and validating the problem does not previously exists. And there is no new TO YOU for the LLM: it can get help from a vast amount of helper domains.

IMHO there's a shot at having category theory really unifying a large chunk of maths in the next decade. It'll be a big ugly ball of Lean, but a queryable one at that.

Top #2 — nfw2:

I've also found it very hard to leave AI agents up to their own devices for long periods and get much productive benefit from it.

I suppose it's possible that frontier labs have internal models that are so far beyond that autonomous research becomes possible, but I'm not sure that's it.

It seems to me like these models are like a very competent, important part of some hypothetical digital brain, but alone they don't have all the facilities they need to be useful, like a genius with severe ADHD and short-term memory loss.

For anything where quality isn't objective in a clear-cut way, very intentional context management is needed to get good outputs. As context size expands, performance degrades. As the number of tasks increases, performance degrees. As the number of independent decisions based on subjective criteria increases, performance degrees.

If you can get a harness that makes sure every decision is made one at a time, focused with only the context it needs, things work great. But making those harnesses is still hard, a lot of work, and something that agents seem to have no clue how to help you with.

↳ reply — nathias:

I don't think its the frontier models, my opus 5.5 has no problem working on a project fairly autonomously, for example if I prompt it in the evening it will work the whole night without issues...

Top #3 — p1necone:

On one hand, yeah, I agree.

On the other hand, using AI to trawl through all the grunt work, experiments, and well trodden areas means I can crawl up pretty close to that giants shoulder and spend way less effort myself answering the actually important questions so I can stand on it.

(This isn't supposed to sound self aggrandising - the giants whose shoulders I'm standing on aren't very tall, and they probably have bigger brothers and sisters, but the idiom was too good of a match to pass up using)

↳ reply 1 — loveparade:

The thing is, without doing the grunt work you usually don't have enough understanding to answer the big questions.

Ask anyone who has an advanced degree in math or physics. They will tell you that doing the boring practice problems over and over is usually the key to understanding, not reading the high level theorems.

↳ reply 2 — Matumio:

The proper term is: "On the shoulders of a very large pyramid of hobbits." The concept is the very core of human intelligence, also known as cultural evolution. I can't resist to recommend Joseph Henrich's book "The Secret of Our Success" every few years here, to anyone interested in human intelligence, and how it is different from other primates.

There was a critical review article with a title that summarizes the book well: "On the shoulders of a very large pyramid of hobbits, or why we are not just very smart chimps. The Secret of Our Success: How Culture is Driving Human Evolution, Domesticating Our Species, and Making Us Smarter." Obviously I got triggered by your comment, which was eerily close to that title.

I worked on modernization in the FAA specifically around digitizing NOTAMs.

I would urge you not to consider this modernization from the perspective you may be familiar, as someone who may work on the bleeding edge and sometimes sees a lack of caution from engineers pushing for change.

The FAAs safety risk management is built around a rigorous process, but that is also a massive slowdown to reasonable progress.

One of the eng I worked with was 80+ years old and just didnt want to retire. He did not understand modern systems at all and the risks we were looking at were not (imo) realistically balanced.

I get the idea that the current administration is pushing safety to the side, but there is another risk where safety becomes a blocker to reasonable change.

When I left that work (more than 15 years ago) it was clearly a blocker.

↳ reply 1 — kalcode:

This isn't like COBOL. Floppy disc were never reliable. They should've been phased out a long time ago

Magnetic degradation, wear from read/write heads, and environmental sensitivity mean disks have a natural expiration date and it's not long. And they are also easy to corrupt from all kinds of magnetic sources around us.

I get other stuff, even DOS like system. Safety critical software/hardware that was battle tested makes sense. Not floppy. Sometime it's just bureaucracy.

my 1980s 5.25" disks still work. i'm surprised but they have laster a long time.

I have distinct memories of copying a project to a floppy in my dorm room, popping the disk out, walking next door (literally next door in the dorms, not even going outside up or down stairs or anything), popping the disk into a team member's PC and the project being gone. We laughed it off and chucked the disk in the trash and got another. Project wasn't lost-lost since I had a copy on my hard disk. This was also the era of the 100MB Zip Drives, which I also had in my PC and thankfully all of our lab PCs had, too. That's what I normally used for all of my day-to-day file transfers of any real import. I still have my zip disks, but I seem to have lost my zip drive, so no idea if the disks still have any data on them.
