Top #1 — DanHulton:

That stained glass whale thing makes me especially grumpy. When it scrolled onto the page, my first thought was "whoah, what a neat idea" and then it was _immediately_ followed by "what a terribly execution."

Like, I'm not even an artist, so I'm sure there's a million things I'm missing, but it's just so upsetting to look at. There's weird random reflections on things that shouldn't have reflections, the coloured light absolutely doesn't actually track through the stained glass onto any surface that makes any sense, light is coming from every which way, it's just... gross to look at for anything more than a quarter of a second.

And this is what they're using to hype people up for it. /shrug

↳ reply — roenxi:

Yeah. I think that the pelican SVG benchmark is actually a much better reflection of the state of AI art than the visual quality of the images.

Based on current trends I would not be at all surprised if LLMs working with tools, SVGs and looking at their own work get there before diffusion models. I've stopped keeping up with the image models so maybe I'm underestimating the progress but I dropped out because they were so frustratingly bad at composition and integrating details together.

That whale image makes me think that the situation hasn't improved as much as I'd expected. It is a really cool idea and a pretty picture, but the whale looks a lot like it is flying over the top of some sort of huge glass dome on the ground.

Top #2 — minimaxir:

Using the grid trick for animations to generate the individual frames has been around for awhile and not specific to ChatGPT: I'm surprised it took this long for one of the official providers to make it explicit. However, adherence between frames is generally tricky, and even in the examples there is a lot of noise between frames although that could be due to compression.

SVG support is interesting but I suspect shenanigans are afoot since that's not how image generation models work, and it would likely strip any SynthID watermarks. It's possible OpenAI has pipelined a raster-to-vector tool that does the conversion automatically. (I developed a similar pipeline and it works extremely well; I'll open source it at some point)

EDIT: Per documentation, there is an explicit `output_format: "svg"`, and I am indeed correct there is raster-to-vector in play:

> The API creates a reference image and uses it to produce the SVG. The quality setting controls that reference image. Decode data[0].b64_json as base64 and save the resulting UTF-8 XML bytes with a .svg extension.

OpenAI claims 50% faster generation with Images 2.6 but curiously price is the same as Image 2.5.

↳ reply 1 — vunderba:

From what I can tell after some preliminary testing, you have to pass an additional large language model to the OpenAI API when generating SVGs.

I couldn't find this requirement in the documentation, but if you don't pass one in, you get this error:

  400 {"message": "SVG generation requires 'svg.model'.",
     "param": "svg.model", "code": "missing_required_parameter"}
I tried it with Sunburst with both gpt-5.5 and gpt-5.6-sol, and the results were nothing spectacular. It’s something you could already do in the ChatGPT interface by asking it to convert an existing image to an equivalent SVG.

https://imgpb.com/bkUrc

Recraft is probably the only group I know of that had a native text-to-SVG generator pretty early on, but since it’s a closed model, I’m not familiar with what they were doing under the hood technically.

https://fal.ai/models/fal-ai/recraft/v4/pro/text-to-vector

↳ reply 2 — padolsey:

Yeh using sprites to make frames consistent (kinda tilting latent space towards a character consistency, zero-shot ~LoRA hack?) is old-school. I did this 3 years ago. https://j11y.io/dance/

Top #3 — preommr:

Feels like ai image generation has plateaud.

Coding related have had massive step-up improvements over time.

The same cannot be said for image generation. If anything, I swear it's gone backwards.

It peaked with very early midjourney (like 2022), maybe follow ups with stable diffusion, and then with some of the nano banana models for actual editing. But overall, very lackluster in comparison to other areas.

↳ reply 1 — vunderba:

There have been a lot of strides in open-weight models, well beyond SDXL. Flux, back in August of 2024 was a game changer, finally allowing us to move past SDXL’s nuclear pile of comma-delimited keywords for prompting and allowing more natural language.

And this summer we got Ideogram V4 and Krea2, both of which are highly capable. You can see how the open/closed models have advanced since SDXL in the Progress tab.

https://genai-showdown.specr.net

MJ is pretty out-of-date by this point though it can still be fun from an image space exploration perspective. It scored a rather pitiful 2 out of 15 on my bench back in the summer of 2025.

↳ reply 2 — mgw:

Your feeling is generally right. There have been no seminal moments in image generation anymore in the last couple of months. Most attention from the big labs has gone to video since that‘s where the money is. We have a page to track the history of it all here https://lumenfall.ai/arena/history

(Right now missing some models which I‘ll add today.)

item.title: A thousand fewer paths to root
item.description: 347 points, 247 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (openai.com)

→ HN comments  ·  347 points  ·  247 comments

Top #1 — darkamaul:

I would be curious to see the distribution of these vulns in the codebase:

- What subsystems are affected?

- What's the median age of the vulnerable code? Is more recent code stronger than old ones?

- What is the type of vulnerabilities found? Memory corruptions, logic bugs, race conditions, ...

This is an impressive result, but we need more info to understand how well this would translate to another codebase, and what lessons can be drawn from this experiment. Not every company has ~million dollards in tokens to spend.

↳ reply — bananaquant:

Good points. Unfortunately, they don't have the people nor the incentive to actually look into that.

Also, let's maybe not call the result impressive until we see what's under the hood.

↳↳ reply — fauigerzigerk:

>Unfortunately, they don't have the people nor the incentive to actually look into that.

These are relatively simple statistics. Some are even trivial. I don't see why it requires any people at all.

It wouldn't even have to be done by OpenAI. Given a list of vulnerabilities, it wouldn't be too hard for third parties to collect these statistics.

Top #2 — Plasmoid:

How did we get to the point where there are a thousand privilege escalation exploits in the kernel?

Is the kernel simply too complex to reason about? Is it an underlying flaw in the security model or language implementation?

Should we assume that all software is more compromised than the kernel?

↳ reply 1 — beala:

Many people seem to be making this about their pet issue, but "these systems are complex" and "the frontier labs have developed models that are superhuman at hacking" seems like a totally sufficient explanation.

I've been working with a LoRa chip called the LR2021. I plugged a dev board into my computer and told Claude to reverse engineer it. He dissected it with a speed and level of efficiency I couldn't believe. Within a few hours, Claude was writing custom patches for a completely opaque patch RAM area meant only for the manufacture. I wrote about it here: https://beala.substack.com/p/your-node-doesnt-need-a-microco...

↳↳ reply — Gigachad:

The stuff we have seen so far feels less like super human hacking skills and more human skills at superhuman scale.

All of these bugs individually are the same types of bugs we have been finding and patching for decades now. But we found a way to scale that far beyond what we had before.

↳ reply 2 — vbezhenar:

That's the drawback of monolithic Linux and tendency to put everything in kernel.

It is absolutely possible to have very minimal kernel with drivers and many other subsystems running with lowered privileges.

That would greatly reduce privilege escalation possibilities. Right now single vulnerability in any kernel subsystem gives you highest access to the system.

Imagine that some USB device driver runs as "nobody:nobody" process having access only to selected syscalls related to its functions. Even if it has vulnerability, you won't go anywhere from there.

Modularity and very granular access controls are the "secret" to secure system.

And the most privileged part of the kernel could be so small that it could be verified with advanced methods, basically proving its correctness.

Top #3 — dangelosaurus:

This is my team’s work. I’m happy to try to answer questions or take questions back to the team.

And we're hiring! https://openai.com/careers/search/?q=cyber

↳ reply 1 — amluto:

Do you have a list of the publicly discussed or fixed ones?

(As someone who used to handle nonpublic Linux kernel security reports and is still very interested in this stuff, I’d love to review a small sample of these reports to get a feel for what kinds of issues are being unearthed.)

Also, please don’t stop at LPEs and information disclosures. If you find cases where Linux can be convinced to misbehave or where the implemented semantics don’t make sense, these are good, too. I’ve found plenty of interesting kernel bugs, including some juicy LPEs, and almost none were memory safety errors :)

↳ reply 2 — BoppreH:

item.title: Residential proxies detected on White House network
item.description: 1065 points, 342 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (layer3intel.com)

→ HN comments  ·  1065 points  ·  342 comments

Top #1 — btown:

The danger here, of course, is that while these compromised devices are currently being monetized in a relatively benign way (other than bandwidth costs to the user, which to be sure can be nontrivial)… it would be naive to assume that there isn't a Command and Control capability that can assign less benign tasking - or can be compromised to do so.

This also puts some of the troubling reports that politicians were bringing phones into SCIFs into context…

↳ reply 1 — mzajc:

> benign

On a server that used to get below 1k HTTP requests a day, I've had several cases of mass scraping from these botnets exceeding 100req/s. The web is getting harder and harder to use due to all the anti-bot mechanisms site operators had to put up.

How is DDOSing every site on the web benign?

↳↳ reply — nucleardog:

Relatively benign.

A compromised device inside the White House network could presumably be doing something _much_ worse than participating in a DDOS against random websites.

↳↳↳ reply — mcv:

And it's right there in the second line of the article:

> One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Surely a Russian company known for cyberattacks against the US having direct access to the White House network is far more serious than just DDOSing random websites. This is espionage at the highest level. (Again.)

↳ reply 2 — _alternator_:

I'll just note that "compromised" is perhaps too strong. These services often come from VPN plugins (eg Hola VPN) that lets users watch sports from different restricted geographic regions. There is a trade here that's in the TOs: you get someone else's IP address, they get yours.

↳ reply 3 — 50208:

Why wouldn't an adversary be using it to conceal command and control traffic?

Top #2 — dhosek:

They’re too polite to say it explicitly, but when they say:

> Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.

There really aren’t very many candidates for who that person might be and it really seems like it would be someone who, I don’t know, maybe lives where the traffic is originating.

↳ reply 1 — dpark:

A lot of people work at the White House. Many of them doubtless work a night shift. The set of candidates here is actually quite large.

↳↳ reply — mrandish:

> A lot of people work at the White House.

I'm no expert but even I've read that "Works at the White House" is bigger than the executive residence and oval office, including the West Wing and the big office building that's directly connected to it by basement walkways. The National Security Council maintains 24-hour watch operations in the Situation Room (which is more a 'complex' than 'room'), while regional desk officers routinely work late evenings to overlap with morning business hours in Europe and Asia.

I asked Gemini if my recollection was correct and got: "The EOP network (managed by the EOP Office of Administration in coordination with Presidential Information Technology Community entities like the White House Communications Agency) operates as a single campus enterprise network. Its high-speed backbone links the West Wing, the EEOB, the East Wing, and nearby administrative facilities such as the New Executive Office Building (NEOB) on 17th Street."

So, definitely an issue that there's a device with some rogue malware installed but the total workforce across all shifts at the White House Complex is roughly between 2,500 and 4,000.

↳↳↳ reply — HaZeust:

"and the big office building that's directly connected to it by basement walkways"

I ask in good faith, but why didn't you just say the Treasury Building?

↳ reply 2 — ajcp:

Even at midnight I can't imagine there being less than 100 people working at the WH in various capacities. While it's probably not the duty/desk officers in the Situation Room/Security Council, there are plenty of maintenance staff that work at night. 5-midnight seems like it overlaps perfectly with a shift schedule.

Top #3 — bronco21016:

Gotta have your SuperBox set up to watch 24 hr cable news working late into the night.

↳ reply 1 — Tangurena2:

For those who don't know what this is, here's a decent podcast about it:

https://darknetdiaries.com/episode/172/

There's a transcript if you want to read, not listen. At the start, you'll be "hey! I gotta get me one!" and later you'll be like "burn it with fire!"

↳↳ reply — yard2010:

> I get a hit in my vulnerability log, like in the threat log on my Palo Alto firewall, and it’s for a SCADA vulnerability. ... A SCADA vulnerability. This makes no sense. SCADA is the control systems used in large-scale industrial settings. Think pumps, valves, conveyor belts, compressors, elevators, railway switches. This is where SCADA systems live. Why in the world is this box that’s here to deliver TV and movies attempting to trigger a SCADA exploit on D3ada55’ network? This is very concerning.

Such things are threats to humanity imho. They can get us back to the times we couldn't exploit the internet to run a society.

↳ reply 2 — JTbane:

I have seen these at mall kiosks advertising "free cable", and today I learned they are proxying from your home network.

Top #2 — thway15269037:

↳ reply 1 — simlevesque:

↳↳ reply — thway15269037:

Yeah, I clicked that too. But knowing qualcomm they obviously cost an arm and a leg. Still interesting how much.

↳ reply 2 — dingdingdang:

Honestly, let me buy one, it's many times faster than the minipc I run local ai on so if the price is right I'm in.

Top #3 — zitterbewegung:

Sort of interesting design It has half a terabyte of SRAM on the accelerator with a 128 GB of RAM replacing HBM with SRAM but keeping regular RAM.

↳ reply — 2001zhaozhao:

half a gigabyte not terabyte lol

↳↳ reply — zrm:

Yeah, this thing is unusual. It resembles a consumer GPU but using normal DRAM with more channels, so then you get more RAM but less memory bandwidth than GDDR/HBM, which is the same thing Apple does. And the TDP is pretty attractive for what it is.

But what is that amount of SRAM for? It simultaneously seems like a lot, because SRAM is so expensive, but still not very much, because what can you fit in 0.5GB? Is there a specific workload that needs something that looks like this?

↳↳↳ reply — tromp:

0.5 GB of SRAM is exactly what the Cuckatoo32 [1] Proof-of-Work scheme needs for optimal solving efficiency. Solutions are 42-cycles in random bipartite graphs of 2^32 edges on 2^32 + 2^32 nodes, which can be found by repeatedly removing edges that have only one adjacent edge. Tracking which nodes have incident edges takes 2^32 (completely randomly accessed) bits which is exactly 0.5GB. Another 0.5 GB is needed to track alive edges but those can be accessed serially for which DRAM suffices.

[1] https://github.com/tromp/cuckoo

I have LED headlights and an LED light bar on my tractor and I can say with 100% confidence that bugs swarm both. To the point I have to wear glasses to keep them out of my eyes if I’m on it for more than about 30 seconds at night.

I’m guessing he’s confusing the dramatic drop in insect life overall with a change in behavior due to different lights.

↳ reply 1 — Izmaki:

I second this. When my home was infested by flies (I stopped counting at ~1000 over a 3 week period) they would always swarm and hang out by my grow lights (full spectrum LEDs) in my kitchen window. It was a great place for fly traps on the flip side.

It is quite possible that flies prefer one part of the light spectrum more than another part, but to say in the title that they don’t swarm at LEDs is misleading at best.

Top #2 — gopalv:

My pet theory is that the dimmable LEDs repel insects (when used as a grow light).

The thing that insects can see and we don't is the rapid flashing of a PWM power controller.

I wonder if these streetlights have power saving fade-ins as the nightfall approaches instead of clicking on at sunset.

Like - https://doi.org/10.1109/CSNT51715.2021.9509652

↳ reply 1 — winrid:

PWM drivers should be banned, the quality of lighting is horrendous and it murders LEDs. You have an rms currernt that is in spec but the peak is way too high.

↳ reply 2 — andai:

One of my favorite things I read growing up was a passage about what it's like to be a fly watching TV.

In those days TV's were big CRT boxes, illuminated by the electron beam which would race across the screen row by row.

A housefly's "refresh rate" on its eyeballs is much higher than that of a human, so the fly wouldn't see an image as we do, but would presumably find it quite relaxing watching the dot of light slowly move across the screen.

Top #3 — dylan604:

I love to shoot long exposure timelapse of the night sky. I set up a couple of LEDs dimmed as low as possible to light a bit of the foreground (over the course of the long exposure the low light adds up so it looks normal for those not familiar). Out of sheer laziness, I just placed them on either side of my tripod. The next day after processing the shot, it was pretty much ruined because of all of the bugs showing up as tracers in each frame.

So, no, not my experience at all.

Bugs don’t just materialize out of the ether to swarm lights. Not to feed swallows. They are there and you will encounter them if the density is much more than zero.

Also better lights don’t necessarily mean perfect lights. We do lots of things to reduce harm. Unfortunately sometimes we do them too much and conserve a significant fraction of the original harm by increasing demand.

item.title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
item.description: 295 points, 108 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ricursive.com)

→ HN comments  ·  295 points  ·  108 comments

Top #1 — advael:

Category narrowing to this degree really has diluted the term "SOTA" quite a lot

You mean it's state of the art for this subset of benchmarks you're targeting? No? Well surely it's state of the art for models of a certain size category? Huh, what about models that are available for local inference? O, state of the art for open models of a certain size made in the US specifically. Uh. Neat!

↳ reply 1 — gpm:

Playing games like this also makes it very easy to accidentally say things that aren't true, like in the headline of the article...

> Introducing Ripple-65B Preview, a Frontier Open-Weight Model

It's not "frontier", it's not "frontier" even in the category of open-weight models (though usually that phrasing would mean frontier over all, and also open weight)... it's only "frontier" in the small sub-category of US made open-weight models.

↳↳ reply — GuB-42:

It is technically frontier, if by "frontier" we mean the Pareto frontier.

Being at the Pareto frontier means that you can't get something better on one aspect without compromising on some other aspect. The trick is that it is easy to be at the Pareto frontier by having enough dimensions.

Here, we have 4: score, number of parameters, origin (US) and open-weight. You can get a better score or a lower number of parameters, but you have to compromise on at least one of the other aspects. That's a pretty weak frontier if you ask me.

↳↳↳ reply — derefr:

“Origin” isn’t part of the Pareto frontier because it’s not a quantitative dimension.

(You could say that “ability to be trusted by US government/military users” is quantifiable, but I would argue that by that metric, this model falls behind non-US-originated open-weight models that have more eyes on them!)

↳ reply 2 — msy:

It's like the Baseball World Series of Frontier models. It's SOTA in the same way Tesla are SOTA EVs - the best you're permitted to buy in the USA.

↳ reply 3 — yorwba:

AFAIK the currently biggest US open-weight model is Inkling, which they include in the comparison, so at least their claim is not limited to a size category. Still they score 0.42 percentage points higher than the second-best model on their chosen benchmark, so it's hardly a meaningful lead.

Top #2 — stewartpark:

It's great to see another competitive open weight model. Congratulations!

But as is, it's probably hard to become popular amongst hobbyists and local model enthusiasts like Qwen's 27B class models or MOE models because it's a 65B dense model and inference will be prohibitively slow on consumer grade hardware, and seems like the goal/mission of the company behind this model is to automate chip design.

So if I have to assume and connect the dots, this is for the companies who want to use AI in air-gapped environments for chip design so that they protect their IPs (not leaking to third party AI labs/hostile parties) and can afford lots of server grade inference hardware for a quick unlock with the big dense model.

Neat!

↳ reply 1 — deepsquirrelnet:

> it's a 65B dense model and inference will be prohibitively slow on consumer grade hardware

Times are changing and with MTP and DFLASH, dense models are back in style. For qwen 3.8 27b, you can get great token generation rates with MTP and for quality, it's much better than a MoE of comparable size.

↳↳ reply — stewartpark:

That helps, yes. But speculative decoding that requires a secondary/draft model means a trade off (smaller KV pool), so often times the only option left is MTP unless you have lots of VRAM. And as you already know, these options (MTP, DFlash, DSpark, etc) are also available for MoE models, too. If it's 3tk/s instead of 1tk/s, we can say it helps but not sure how many people would be excited about that. I'd be more excited about 150tk/s instead of 50tk/s!

↳ reply 2 — 59nadir:

Is it competitive overall or just competitive when compared to "U.S. Open-Weight models that are otherwise pretty decent at agentic coding"? The latter does not imply the former.

Top #3 — wmf:

Congratulations I guess but it's a pretty bad look to not even mention those other open weight models.

↳ reply 1 — karmakaze:

What's funnier is that after cherry picking models for comparison, they further cherry picked Inking for size comparison instead of better and smaller Beam 1.0

The bar chart also shows Nemotron 3 Ultra instead of smaller and better Nemotron 3.5 Super.

item.title: Show HN: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander
item.description: 193 points, 25 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (fireflyk64.github.io)

→ HN comments  ·  193 points  ·  25 comments

Top #1 — daniel_rh:

Author here: in 2015, I was playing the classic Wing Commander in DOSBox and suddenly realized the game state fit in the 64k data segment.

Over ten years my brother and I went through a set of experiments (stop and go, turn, communicate) while probing the memory. We uncovered where the variables were, how to inject calls into the game functions, and how to sync the gamestate across the network, so we can fly the story missions together.

My favorite finding is that the camera lives in entity slot 0x3D, which is possibly a "3D" reference by the original developers.

You can play it at https://fireflyk64.github.io/dosbox in browser. If you own Wing Commander, drag in the installer since no game files are hosted. If you don't, the page will load the original DOS/3Dfx version of Vega Strike, before I open sourced it. I upscaled and redid DOS Vega Strike art using AI, but it now has multiplayer and a similar feel.

I'll be in the lobby for the next few hours if anyone wants to fly together.

Disclosure: I also used AI for the final step to help compile for the browser and port our TCP networking stack to WebRTC with voice and solve a few lingering bugs.

↳ reply 1 — cadr:

I don't know if I'm more impressed with the result, or that you kept coming back to it for a decade. Super cool!

↳ reply 2 — frikk:

helllllll yeah. i think it's awesome when domain experts and clever humans use AI to automate the implementation after they've designed the path through the forest. Nice work.

Top #2 — herodoturtle:

What a brilliantly fun project to share with the world. Thank you to the authors.

Top #3 — Tepix:

Neat! You're using the data channel for voice? why not the rtc stream?

↳ reply — daniel_rh:

Thanks for the feedback! I'll have a look. I do worry about congestion coupling since it would mean a bursty voice stream could affect game packets. Keeping it on a different stream allows game data priority over voice.

item.title: Education shouldn't be held for ransom
item.description: 126 points, 83 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blog.kagi.com)

→ HN comments  ·  126 points  ·  83 comments

Top #1 — SeanAnderson:

I haven't felt as concerned about this news article as others.

IME, schools really don't have a good grasp on what AI means in relationship to them and what policies would result in better outcomes.

I work in the ed tech parent-teacher communication space. We offer automatic translations of communication to other languages via Google Translate. Google Translate uses AI. Schools come to us and tell us we need to disable all our AI features. We do. Then they freak out asking where their feature went. We explain. They say they don't want to lose translations they just don't want to deal with "AI stuff"

It's not clear to me if this stance from Google is a new thing. Did they recently add AI to search and are trying to use bundling behaviors to incept AI into areas it wouldn't be? Or did policy recently become rabid against the use of AI without fully appreciating the ask and ramifications? Both?

↳ reply 1 — SamBam:

Schools want to control whether Gemini and other generative AI is available to students.

I'm a middle school science teacher. We've already moved much of our work to paper because of this issue, but there is so much good science that should be done using computer simulations and other tools. So I do have computers out for some lessons.

So now, on a lesson where a computer is out, a student can instantly type in a question on the Google search bar, get an AI answer, and write it down with zero thoughts traveling through their heads.

Yes, redesign the lesson. Yes, if computers are out don't ask questions that an AI can answer. But you know what? Instead of needing to cut out everything that makes a lesson a productive struggle for kids, it would be great just to not have Gemini cheat for them.

↳↳ reply — mikeleeorg:

> Schools want to control whether Gemini and other generative AI is available to students.

I really wish more articles and social media posts point this out, but a lot of writers either don't know this distinction or are going with a more "clickbaity" angle on purpose.

↳ reply 2 — stevemk14ebr:

This is basically pedantry, they want generative AI and AI search off. If anyone is confused then you should be asking more questions to understand the desires.

↳ reply 3 — paxy:

Yeah it's pretty likely that schools are adding strict no AI clauses in their Google Workplace contracts and Google's lawyers are including search in that definition just to be safe. If they then want to enable it manually, sure.

Top #2 — danielciocirlan:

Education is going to be left in tatters after AIs creep into every facet of (tech-enabled) life.

Big tech doesn’t care about teaching people to think. All the money is in the capture of attention, and AI will only make everything 100x more convenient and a no-brainer (quite literally) to pick the hard way of thought and effort for just about anything… as long as the user is caught. Education has fundamentally the opposite goal.

↳ reply — beezlebroxxxxxx:

> Education is going to be left in tatters

Public, free education will. People who can afford it are sending their kids to schools with very strict technology policies, stricter than what is possible in many public schools nowadays (for a number of reasons).

It's very much a "for the masses" mindset with the people who gain from this kind of relationship between technology and public schools.

↳↳ reply — JuniperMesos:

Public free education is already in tatters in many neighborhoods and has been for many decades. People already pay a lot of money to live in a neighborhood with expensive housing prices in order to price out from living there people whose children would make the local public school worse (by e.g. getting into physical fights). People sometimes pay for a private school to avoid this because it is cheaper than a house in a neighborhood with people whose children make good students to spend time in close physical proximity with.

Top #3 — ahmedfromtunis:

It's ironic that Kagi uses confusion (as to not say deception) to market itself as the more ethical brand.

Google clarified that admins can turn on and off each of the options independently, including search without AI.

I don't like to defend trillion-dollar companies in my free time, but what Kagi is trying to do with this piece is not good.

↳ reply — kelgan:

Hi there -- I wrote this post. What's deceptive about it? I mentioned that Google walked it back some and even link to it. But what educators that I've spoken to want is no AI Overviews in Google Search, which still isn't an option.

item.title: A new Go API for JSON
item.description: 231 points, 96 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (go.dev)

→ HN comments  ·  231 points  ·  96 comments

Top #1 — asim:

At this stage to me Go is the new C compiler. Quite honestly I spent 10 years or more writing Go code. At times 18 hours a day. And now with AI, I get models to write my Go code. I STILL want it to be Go code. Is that strange? No because I understand the performance and safety of Go. But I rarely write it directly anymore. Probably not at all in 6-9 months. Yet I still occasionally look at the code to see what the output looks like.

So yea hopefully a nice new addition but only my prompts now matter. So need to make sure they pickup on the new API.

↳ reply 1 — egnehots:

Truly the argument can be made either way.

If you code in Go, the code is more high level, prettier, simpler.

If you code in Rust, the code is more robust, efficient, faster.

Both are important for LLM, why can't we have a high level, simple language that is also robust, efficient and fast? =)

↳↳ reply — andriy_koval:

> Both are important for LLM, why can't we have a high level, simple language that is also robust, efficient and fast? =)

I think many variants from Rust can be stripped to make it simple, especially in type system, which is way more complicated than go.

↳↳↳ reply — nonethewiser:

I dont think we need simpler types for agentic coding though. We need compiler speed. I guess those are probably related to some degree though.

↳ reply 2 — biztos:

As I do more agentic coding, I am starting to feel strongly that I need to set aside a project -- and time -- for strictly hand-coding, using AI (if at all) only to explain things, never to write any code.

First, I like programming and don't want to stop doing it just because a machine can do it too. Second, I'm pretty sure atrophied coding skills will make me worse at directing the machines, thus worse at what seems to be "the job" these days.

↳ reply 3 — jacobgold:

I still prefer Go over the alternatives because I'm reviewing the code carefully and trying to make it all look as good as if I'd written it very carefully by hand.

The few times I've needed a language without a GC and used Rust and C as target languages, I've reviewed the code less and enjoyed it less.

Top #2 — brunoborges:

> "JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format [...]"

Clearly it isn't, otherwise every language would have sorted it out by... a long time ago.

↳ reply 1 — kccqzy:

Some languages have a culture of doing things correctly and conforming strictly to the spec. These languages have indeed sorted it out years ago. Haskell for example. Any language that doesn’t have a special number type for JSON is a half-assed implementation, because 1e1000 is a perfectly valid JSON number that is beyond the typical IEEE754 double precision floating point numbers; does your language handle that correctly? Haskell does. This is but a small example of a strong culture bias towards correctness.

↳↳ reply — layer8:

The spec (RFC 8259) leaves significant leeway to implementations:

A JSON parser MAY accept non-JSON forms or extensions.

An implementation may set limits on the size of texts that it accepts. An implementation may set limits on the maximum depth of nesting. An implementation may set limits on the range and precision of numbers. An implementation may set limits on the length and character contents of strings.

Add to that things like duplicate keys being allowed by the spec. There’s a lot of implementation choices to decide on.

And then things can get really complex with JSON Schema.

↳↳↳ reply — kccqzy:

Yeah that’s what I mean by strictly. Does your implementation take shortcuts or does it hold itself to a higher standard and not do that? Does it only use available memory as the ultimate limit?

A lot of specs contain these optional limitations. The C standard allowed implementations to truncate variable names to 31 characters if they have external linkage and 63 if internal linkage. Would you be happy if your implementation actually does that? Of course not. Neither LLVM nor GCC does that. That’s because people writing compilers also hold themselves to a higher standard. Now imagine this kind of attitude being pervasive.

↳ reply 2 — ivanjermakov:

Simple data format does not imply that API to work with it is easy to get right.

Top #3 — CamouflagedKiwi:

I generally like `encoding/json/v2` and I'm glad they did it.

I wish they'd left `MarshalIndent` in there though. The equivalent code is super complicated and non-obvious, so it's a pain to migrate, and it's a pain when you're banging out some quick code and want to dump some readable JSON. I suppose these days the LLMs can write the complicated version for us, of course.

↳ reply 1 — athorax:

I'm not sure if I'm missing something, but isn't this functionality just moved into jsontext? https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json/jsontext#Value.Indent

  v := jsontext.Value(b)
  v.Indent()
  fmt.Println(string(v))

↳↳ reply — irq-1:

    func WithIndent(indent string) Options
https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json/jsontext#WithIndent

↳ reply 2 — arccy:

    json.Marshal(v, jsontext.WithIndent("  "))

?

item.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
item.description: 175 points, 85 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (anthropic.com)

→ HN comments  ·  175 points  ·  85 comments

Top #1 — ljlolel:

already solved provable inference with encrypted chats on trustedrouter (using TEEs which most people don’t know about)

Top #2 — vessenes:

I've been writing about the need for provable inference (and training) on and off for a number of years; this is welcome news and a good start, and a significant improvement on prior zk results.

The problems of inference proof for a closed model provider are more difficult than an open model provider -- you can get a probabilistic proof much more cheaply out of four independent inference providers running the same non-batched prompt than this 90-100x compute hit.

Anthropic and others also have a significant problem with these proofs in that they have a lot of incentive internally to have some portions of the pre-prompt secret; I haven't read this newest scheme closely enough to determine if they have a way to hide parts of the prompt with the proof. But if they don't, they are almost certainly not going to want to send these proofs out in the general case.

Last, I'll take this moment to soapbox and say for the researchers out there -- provable inference is nice. Provable training corpus information would be spectacular. It would be very, very, very nice to provide a set of model weights and a proof that they had only been trained on a dataset. To be clear, this is a really hard problem, but it would change fundamentally what levels of trust we could have about a given set of weights.

↳ reply 1 — mike_hearn:

> It would be very, very, very nice to provide a set of model weights and a proof that they had only been trained on a dataset. To be clear, this is a really hard problem, but it would change fundamentally what levels of trust we could have about a given set of weights.

Is it hard? Seems like it isn't that hard if you use NVIDIA's remote attestation/enclave support instead of trying to do everything with ZKPs which have always been something of a dead end. CC overhead 2%, ZKP 100x+ and gigabyte sized proofs - just for inference. It's never been competitive.

I'm very skeptical anyone would care about this for training though. I mean, if there's someone out there who genuinely really really wants proofs of the dataset used to train model weights, let's talk? But it seems the value is mostly for open weights inference providers. They can prove what weights they're serving and they can prove they can't see people's prompts. It would take a lot of the risk out of using a no-name LLM cloud service.

Unfortunately, after many years of this stuff I have become old and cynical. The stated/revealed preference mismatch is huge. The majority of people say they want privacy in theory but in practice won't trade anything off to get it, and especially not convenience.

↳↳ reply — lrvick:

> The majority of people

Most do not even realize they have a choice and are not educated enough to make the one in their own best interest. Fast food wins as a staple for many people over a healthy home cooked meal.

Creating healthy and safe choices and making them the default is some of the most important work there is.

↳ reply 2 — cmrx64:

I have been addressing this problem head on aggressively; https://github.com/emberian/whatember is the toplevel index. Things like arithmetizing parser/other automata to write semantic predicates (incl graph rewrites!) over training sets, inference requests, etc.

Top #3 — gopalv:

> In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers?

> the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.

> The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads (and 21 seconds on a single thread), including the offline phase's check

I know they mentioned $ETH in the technical report, but this is exactly the mechanic for a crypto currency Proof-of-Work which is expensive by design.

When they announced it, I was hoping for a 5% overhead validation that the model that served you is really Fable and not Opus.

The quantization bit caught me out, because we saw the boundary crossing from good-context-size to bad is so sharp it feels like longer context requests are sent to quantized models to make more room for more KV-Cache. This would expose those sorts of tricks people can play to have the same GPU do better on short context benchmarks and gracefully degrade on long context.

At work, we did a bit of digging[1] into exactly why BaseTen, Fireworks and Together serve Inkling weights differently, we suspected the issue was a combination of how you do disaggregated prefill (+streaming) and quantization for longer context tasks.

[1] - https://isotopes.ai/blog/everyone-is-selling-the-same-model-...

↳ reply — shakow:

No, that has nothing to do with PoW. PoW is computing something intrinsically useless but very hard just to prove you spent all that time, but trivial to check.

ZkPs are expensive to check and even more so to generate because the problem is intrinsically very compute heavy. The ecosystem would immediately jump into a faster way of doing thing, compute time are seen as a flaw, not a feature.

item.title: 'It's just vape, nail, charity shops': Can anything save UK high street?
item.description: 130 points, 323 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (theguardian.com)

→ HN comments  ·  130 points  ·  323 comments

Top #1 — guystone:

It comes down to money and the cost of living. Landlords are extracting rent, no room for entrepreneurship.

A race to the bottom, but I wouldn’t blame Amazon. Large multinational chains were hollowing out high streets and making them less pleasant before online shopping.

As another comment said, councils and government should treat high streets more like public commons, prioritising independent businesses and making places distinctive.

What frustrates me is that even prosperous areas with new developments rarely make space for small businesses. Instead, we get “private equity” chain.

Ugh, one I saw recently was Bristol University’s new campus by Temple Meads. The wall between the campus and station could have been lined with small, affordable units for independent and student-run businesses. Would love to browse a few interesting shops or grab a decent sandwich before catching a late train. 23m for a new entrance but where are the opportunities. (This is based off the media announcements, not walked through there yet)

↳ reply 1 — slibhb:

> councils and government should treat high streets more like public commons, prioritising independent businesses and making places distinctive.

You're advocating central planning.

The real problem is that it's very hard to build stuff in the UK. This is a choice that the people have made and the status quo still continue until they choose differently.

↳↳ reply — AnthonyMouse:

> You're advocating central planning.

Central planning is the status quo. That's essentially what zoning rules are, and why everything is such a mess. You want to open a shop and live above it? No, sorry, not zoned for residential; banned. Operate the shop out of your house instead? Haha, banned. What if your shop really doesn't need very much space at all, so something the size of a closet would do as long as it's in the right location? Nope, minimum unit sizes or similar, prohibited by law. And so on.

If they want to stop doing this that would be great, but if they're not going to stop doing it then having the rules be things like "no chains" instead of "no small units" would certainly be an improvement.

↳↳↳ reply — roryirvine:

Zoning in the American sense doesn't exist in the UK, outside of Local Development Orders and (maybe, if you squint a bit) the system of Brownfield Land Registers.

Outside those very limited exceptions, planning in the UK is done on a discretionary basis, and both the discretionary system and the LDOs are overseen by Local Planning Authorities made up of elected local councillors.

There's no central planning authority, and the system is designed to be flexible at the cost of providing less certainty to developers. Mixed use developments are the norm here, and most new residential blocks will have some form of commercial or social space on the ground floor.

↳ reply 2 — specproc:

I rent a workspace outside of my home, I'm paying less than 150 quid for a room in a light industrial zone. Gives me space for my fun stuff as well as work. I love having my own space, and it's very affordable.

I was just looking at the prices for city centre commercial rental in my nearest town. Huge spaces available, it's generally more per month, and I'd be worried about the rates threshold, but at a lower price point we'd be in business.

I think there's something to that. More people using a centre for work would create more opportunities in towns.

Again, I think the challenge the UK has is the gross differential between incomes and the cost of buying or renting property. Unsustainable, and very much part of these morbid symptoms.

↳ reply 3 — motbus3:

That is a very valid point. However, I suspect that some of the businesses that managed to survive transitioned into operations that function solely as fulfillment centers for dispatching packages.

The issue with that approach is that it results in numerous vacant spaces, which fail to attract enough foot traffic to be appealing to other businesses.

There was a struggling shopping mall near my home. Many retailers left the premises after one of the big stores shut down. Recently some other big brand occupied the space, in a couple of months besides it there is a Samsung store and an apple store. Now all spaces are busy and they stay busy all week long.

This makes me suspect that we highly optimised for the "2010s" online era without considering the side effects.

Top #2 — Lio:

Commercial property on our high streets is owned, in the main, by foreign investment firms that treat it as an asset.

In many cases you can’t find out who the owner is. There’s too many shell companies involved.

These firms don’t care about occupancy, they care about the resale book value.

Business tax rates are based on those property valuations.

There’s no chance the property companies will reduce the value of their portfolio to reduce burden for tenants they don’t care about.

Then you have foreign online retailers like Amazon and Temu able to use complex multinational tax avoidance schemes and fake products to undercut the high street.

How can you compete if Amazon can deliver a knock off from China, that you can’t legally sell, faster than you can stock a real one into the shop, and at half the price?

↳ reply — jeffrallen:

> How can you compete

Convince your neighbors that it's better to buy products they know from producers they trust from neighbors they live near.

It's small town and old school, but I don't see any other solution.

↳↳ reply — Lio:

I agree. Every pound spent locally massively benefits society.

If good shops are available people will use them, if they provide what they're looking for.

I think we need the government to look at how retail works and what shoppers actually want.

There's not much local shops can do about the long tail, they can't stock everything. At the very least need to stop penalising them financially and allowing online retailers to compete on tax avoidance.

My father is old and naive. He was tricked into ordering fake "Yorkshire" tea bags from Temu. Fake tea bags for gods sake. It would be funny if it wasn't so tragic.

We have no control on the quality coming from these sites. We can't even guarantee items are not made using slavery. Both Temu and Chien executives refused to reveal that in parliamentary investigations.

Stuff like that has to stop, standards needs to be universally applied or the bad will drive out the good.

Top #3 — nickdothutton:

UK high streets have been in some kind of decline (IMO) for decades now. Long before online shopping, COVID and its repercussions, and the current wave of street crime (phones, watches) and front businesses (vape and phone repair shops hiring dozens of "skilled" workers on visas... to work in a tiny cupboard unit with implausible turnover). Even when a new "luxury" apartment block is constructed, the retail units often remain vacant for years before being occupied by a constantly changing list of tenants, none of which seem to be able to make a success of it. The nursery becomes a dojo, which becomes a social enterprise cafe, which eventually becomes an estate agent, which then closes.

Rents are high, parking difficult, the products undifferentiated (carbon copy list of the same 15-20 chain franchises), not unique. After all of that, I'll assume prices are no better and may be worse than online retail.

I'm not sure what the answer is, as retail is not my area of expertise. However I think that if there is a solution it will have something to do with people, community, and offering a specifically local experience. Not one which is purely a chore, and I think it will involve much more than just "convenience".

item.title: AMD expects to outsell Intel in Q4 for the first time in history
item.description: 475 points, 174 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (tomshardware.com)

→ HN comments  ·  475 points  ·  174 comments

Top #1 — mickeyp:

That says more about Intel's shambolic efforts than it does about AMD's road to damascus moment.

Honestly both of them have demonstrated that they have little interest in AI. Intel gave up on Optane right as (a much-improved successor) would've helped with MoE offsetting or even as a highly durable drive for KV caching.

AMD have... turned out some decent gaming graphics cards and fine server CPUs but little else.

People are out there solding SMDs on old Nvidia mining rig GPUs to use them for inference; their hardware is not depreciating at the normal rate you'd expect from GPUs. DGX spark is finally useful now that AI can write multi-machine inference tooling optimised to it. Where's AMD in all of this? Nowhere.

↳ reply 1 — zdw:

AMD has their Strix/Gorgon Halo as a competitor to DGX Spark, which is at least in the ballpark in terms of bandwidth, and being x86 has some compatibility benefits.

If you wanted a GPU with 32GB of memory for AI tasks, the AMD AI Pro R9700 was (up until about a month ago) reasonably priced at ~$1300. It's not a RTX 5090 in terms of bandwidth and compute, but for the price and being actually purchasable it's a reasonable pick.

↳↳ reply — mickeyp:

I like to think that if there are wins to be had, the market will price that in.

Those cards are cheap because they're not really that amazing.

↳↳↳ reply — wmf:

This is somewhat true. A lot of AMD hardware is underpriced at launch because ROCm doesn't work yet. Then once ROCm is working the price moves up to what it should be.

↳ reply 2 — Twirrim:

For what it's worth, AMD is very actively pushing GPU hardware, particularly towards the hyperscalers. From what I've seen, they're really focusing in on the large quantity end users (your OpenAI, Meta, etc. types), presumably because they'll have the technical expertise and willingness to collaborate with them on issues as long as the GPUs are cheap enough.

↳ reply 3 — mort96:

I never understood why some fraction of technologists seem convinced that Optane was this amazing thing that would've been awesome if only Intel hadn't killed it.

It never made sense. It's slower than RAM, and what do I get for it? Persistence? I don't want persistent RAM, I like the ability to reboot to solve problems, and storing stuff on a non-volatile mediums has all sorts of legal implications which it's easier to avoid.

It's more expensive and has less storage than SSDs, even though the main downside of SSDs is their high price per gigabyte and relatively low capacities.

It's going in the wrong direction for both use cases. I guess it could have a very niche use case as a super fast persistent caching layer in front of spinning rust but that's kinda it.

Top #2 — davoneus:

Having strong competition between the CPU vendors is always a good thing. AMD has made mistakes, but it's hard to argue they don't deserve to outsell Intel for a change.

↳ reply 1 — deepsquirrelnet:

I have reservations about AMD due to repeatedly poor Linux support. My 8700GE APU has display freezes and can't recover 1-2 times a week. For a chip that was released 2.5y ago, that's nuts.

↳ reply 2 — theandrewbailey:

I hope they use much of this windfall to invest in improved products in the future. It's unlikely to impossible that Radeon or Instinct will ever be more popular or faster than its competition, but it shouldn't languish, and the Zen series should keep running circles around Intel.

Top #3 — p1necone:

The vibes I'm getting are that x86 is on its way out - apple switched, and mainstream laptops are releasing with fast snapdragon chips - I'm thinking both Intel and AMD risk becoming obsolete if they keep focusing on x86 chips.

Anyone with insight into the industry know how much institutional knowledge would be relevant still with an ISA switch?

↳ reply — layer8:

Windows-on-ARM market share seems to be stagnating at a low-ish single-digit percentage, I don’t see it overtaking x86 anytime soon.

↳↳ reply — SR2Z:

↳↳↳ reply — largbae:

Most enterprises capable of running that much gear won't take that risk even if it is unenforceable. Oracle has made a great living threatening audits of companies who download its updates.

↳ reply 2 — FuriouslyAdrift:

We're running Kimi 2.8 on a 4x AMD MI300A single server on-premise that cost about $110k.

We will break even from our old Claude spend in about 2 weeks.

It services 30-40 analysts and staff concurrently and is faster than any of the SaaS out there for us.

↳ reply 3 — joecot:

The benefit is that you can use these models on a variety of different providers. You're not stuck with a single proprietary provider. Aggregators like OpenCode Zen and OpenCode Go can shop around providers on these. OpenRouter shows you the costs of a bunch of the providers, and you can route to the cheapest ones.

I regularly use together.ai with models like this, where they're fully self hosting them and I can turn off all data retention, at a fraction of the cost of proprietary models. I recently discovered abliterated models (models edited to not refuse to work on security stuff) and hosts for them like refuseless.com, and that's an option for open source models, not for proprietary ones.

Top #2 — segmondy:

Doesn't seem to outpace DeepSeekV4.1-Flash by much. Hy4 also announced their models and they have tons of internal benchmark, and K3.1 doesn't score that high on those benchmarks whereas Opus5.5 does, so it seems K3.1 is benchmaxxed.

↳ reply 1 — reissbaker:

If you use it day-to-day you can definitely feel that K3 (and K3.1) are much stronger than DS4.1-Flash-1017. There's something the benchmarks don't capture. DS4.1-Flash-1017 is an amazing model for the price, but it's not a very large model in comparison.

I wouldn't over-weight internal benchmarks from a competitor that claim benchmaxxing TBH. Kimi K3 has been at the top of Design Arena for open-weight models for a long long time, and I suspect K3.1 will be there for a long time too. item.title: A wave of plastic-free coffee pods and machines
item.description: 132 points, 155 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (cnn.com)

→ HN comments  ·  132 points  ·  155 comments

Top #1 — troyvit:

Huh, cool. If you want to save a few bucks you can go with a stainless steel French press or a mason jar if you're into cold brews. You're symbolizing a different kind of status though.

This summer was sunny and hot in Colorado, so every morning I'd make a jar of sun coffee. I'd leave it out through the day and overnight. The next morning I'd pull it in, filter it, refill it with grounds and water and take it outside again. It was cool enough to enjoy and really smooth.

↳ reply 1 — throwaway81523:

French press coffee isn't so healthy either because of stuff like cafestols in the fines (small diameter grounds) that slip through the french press screen. To get rid of those you want a brewing scheme with a paper filter. The simplest no-plastic approach is a Chemex. They have a history and they also look cool as heck. Unfortunately, since they are made of glass, they can break if you're not careful. https://chemexcoffeemaker.com/

↳↳ reply — seatac76:

The Chemex filter do tend filter out more of the subtle coffee flavor. I find V60 to be the right balance in flavor and ease of use.

↳ reply 2 — hedora:

If you want to save fewer bucks, get to zero plastic and get better espresso, you can buy one of these and a burr grinder:

https://flairespresso.com/products/the-flair-classic

I've had one for about a decade. It reliably produces better espresso than >99% of Bay Area coffee shops. (>95% if you exclude national chains).

If I were buying one today, I'd toss the flow control head, silicon sleeve on the cylinder and the pressure gauge, but those come with it for free now, so to each their own, I guess.

The trick is to boil the stainless steel cylinder in your kettle (PID at sea level, conventional above ~ 2000 ft elevation) with the water so that you get the temperature dialed in within a degree C or so, like a conventional (lead-filled, unlike the flair) Italian machine. I use a pair of tongs to pick up the stainless steel cylinder, so I don't need the sleeve. (Check the boiling point of water at your elevation -- unlike a steam machine, this can't exceed that temperature, so stuff might start to run kinda cool at 3000 ft or so).

Flair doesn't sell a "true" classic anymore, but I bet they could get the bare bones variant I use to < $100 if they tried. Maybe someone else will when any patents run out. My only other complaint is that the two-in-one bottomless porta-filter I have runs the espresso across plastic when in non-bottomless mode.

Note that the thing I linked has a plastic plunger. They make a stainless steel one as an upgrade. At that point, you're down to one silcone o-ring in the water / coffee path. Everything else is stainless, so no lead. The next thing to worry about is nickel, but that only matters if you're allergic. I used to use the SS plunger, but then you need to boil it too if you want to dial in the water temperature.

↳ reply 3 — asdff:

When I broke my french press I got by fine with just throwing grounds in a pot of boiled water and decanting it off after a few minutes steep. Basically all the press does anyhow just less convenient.

Top #2 — seemaze:

Hate to be the bearer of bad news, but even the $10k slayer espresso machine has a plastic water resevoir. Granted the brewing assembly is mostly plastic free.

While I sympathize with the sentiment to eliminate plastic from the transport chain for anything ingestible, it's practically impossible in the modern world.

Simple is usually best; glass or ceramic pour over, stainless press, or even the traditional South American coffee sock[0]

[0]https://perfectdailygrind.com/2016/01/coffee-sock-old-school...

↳ reply 1 — benrutter:

> While I sympathize with the sentiment to eliminate plastic from the transport chain for anything ingestible, it's practically impossible in the modern world.

I think the argument is pretty simple:

- Plastic is bad (environment, microplastics, etc) - We should minimize it

That doesn't necessitate a "all the way to zero or don't bother" logic, which what you're saying reads as.

Coffee pods machines have been an environmental nightmare, great to see a growing trend that addresses this.

↳ reply 2 — Kirby64:

> Hate to be the bearer of bad news, but even the $10k slayer espresso machine has a plastic water resevoir. Granted the brewing assembly is mostly plastic free.

There's some people that care about no plastic at all anywhere (which... is pretty unrealistic considering water pipes are plastic), but usually the primary concern is plastic in the heated water portions. Water tanks on espresso machines are not typically heated.

Top #3 — mikeweiss:

I like Moka pots. Zero plastic

But seriously it's a shame how hard it is to find products like coffee makers and electric kettles with no plastic. Heat and plastic don't mix

↳ reply 1 — asdff:

Took me forever to find a french press that was all glass and stainless steel. Most of them the little filter at the cap (which vintage ones lack entirely fwiw) is some black plastic, but I found a bodum off crate and barrel a couple years ago that was stainless for that part too.

> Heat and plastic don't mix

actually they do, and that's the problem

Top #1 — chmod775:

Students at my university in Berlin need to cross a busy road to travel between campus areas, which meant jaywalking or a long trip to a crossing with traffic lights down the road. A steady stream of students late to their next class sprinting across a six lane road is not great.

At some point students started painting their own crosswalk, which would be removed again and again by authorities, until the city eventually got the hint and installed a permanent crosswalk with a traffic light and a pedestrian island.

Sometimes the way to get something is fixed is by demonstrating the fix.

↳ reply 1 — michaelt:

One such report (in German): https://www.rbb24.de/politik/beitrag/2025/10/zebrastreifen-e... in Eberswalde; apparently firefighters were called in to remove the paint but were unsuccessful in their attempts to wash away the white stripes, and police launched an investigation into suspected interference with road traffic.

And another in Dresden: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cQUpQZAeA3w https://www.diesachsen.de/en/politics/a-zebra-crossing-in-dr... "In the summer of 2025, unknown individuals painted a crosswalk on the roadway along the busy street in Neustadt to provide safe access to the Heinrich Schütz Conservatory. The city promptly blocked off the crossing with warning cones [...] stating that unauthorized crosswalks constitute not only property damage but also a dangerous interference with traffic. Furthermore, traffic signs installed without authorization constitute an administrative offense under the Road Traffic Code."

In Los Angeles https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-16/risking-... "Risking arrest, he paints illicit crosswalks across L.A. ‘We can’t wait any longer’" (initially repainting faded crosswalks, rather than creating new ones)

item.title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?
item.description: 338 points, 376 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article

→ HN comments  ·  338 points  ·  376 comments

Top #1 — tomburgs:

1.) None anymore. They're all turning into increasingly poor value for (my) money. I need AI on my own schedule and don't want to be paying for compute I don't need and end up waiting for limits to reset when I do need it. If I was to use one though it'd probably be Opencode Go.

2.) Yes, I'm currently using OpenRouter. It's good for quickly switching around and trying different models, but I currently have it constrained to just 3 models and 1 provider. Truthfully I could just use that provider directly, but I like retaining some flexibility.

3.) I've been using OpenCode for over a year. I think it's an incredible tool and its wide support is a massive boon. It's really easy to pull in skills, tag the skills, and switch providers. Their more recent changes into turning the CLI into more of a GUI has been quite annoying (wdym I have to tap an X in my CLI to close a tab), but not enough for me to (yet) look elsewhere.

4.) Nope, no idea what those are but thanks for teaching me about something new.

5.) In EU (DK) so we don't get access to Dots or Muse like everyone else. I have used Grok Bot and I really like it. It's super helpful and I'm using it as a personal assistant. I delegate tasks to it that I just can't be bothered doing manually or can't figure out easily (e.g using some accounting tools, figuring out cryptic documentation, etc.). I've also used Hermes Agent, but I didn't like it as much. It's great intent but the UI/UX is really not it. It looks like it was taken out of a 90s hacker movie and I'm sure some people like it, but I prefer tools that look polished and focused. I might switch back to it though if something was to happen to Grok Bot.

P.S the models I primarily use are DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash. If you use skills to their full potential they feel SotA to me (my reference point for SotA being OpenAI models we use at work, since we have an enterprise agreement).

Top #2 — jvidalv:

At work I main Opus 5.5 on Claude Desktop app. I have joined my current job 2 months ago and I literally never opened any IDE.

Personally I own a Ultra plan on Claude and a 200 plan on Codex (400 dollars month).

I run them from their native desktop apps, no longer I use any terminal app to run them.

I have not opened a IDE for months now, any diff I need to check I use the Github PR.

In the personal level I use the agents for everything, basically the only thing that I still do on my computer outside of agents is consuming content like HackerNews, random forums, reddit or youtube. All the rest: sending emails, reading them, filling forms, configuring apis, submitting apps to stores ( run a couple of successful mobile apps), building them... Is all done by the agents on my behalf.

Crazy world we live in eh?

Top #3 — Animats:

Embarrassingly, I don't have one yet. I'm mostly still writing code one keystroke at a time. I've used Github Copilot to translate between languages and look things up, but haven't trusted it to write new code or fix anything.

Claude Fable is now good enough that I should be using it. The latest Claude version is said to be comparable to a mid-career graphics programmer, which is about what I need. Six months ago it wasn't good enough to use for such work, and probably would have made a hash of my code. There's been progress.

But Anthropic's business practices are scary. They have a reputation for cancelling accounts for random reasons, offer rather bad terms, and have no customer support. I have a strong aversion to services with a reputation for cancelling services arbitrarily. They will apparently cancel based on their system's guesses as to what you're working on. Sometimes they guess wrong. What I'm doing (metaverse clients) is so far out of the mainstream they may guess wrong.

I'm currently stalled signing up for Claude because their verification email system can't get to my inbox. (Some problem with their using Constant Contact, a spam system, to send transactional emails to my own domain, which, long ago, I had blocked at the Constant Contact end. I think. The verification email never touches the inbound mail server.) It's very important to Anthropic that you sign up with the "right" email address, and it may not be possible to change it, so using some disposable address is not a good idea.

Suggestions?

↳ reply 1 — ChrisRR:

You don't even need to start off with Fable. Give Opus 5.5 a try first and then then try Fable if you feel like you need to push it further

↳ reply 2 — computomatic:

You can access Claude models through any number of providers - OpenRouter, AWS Bedrock, etc. and as far as I know, Claude Code can be used with any of them. The only real benefit to going direct through Anthropic is the subscriptions. It’s worth the risk for the discount, but if you get locked out, there’s other (pricy) options to get unblocked.

item.title: US voters roundly reject data centers in ballot measures
item.description: 310 points, 625 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (semafor.com)

→ HN comments  ·  310 points  ·  625 comments

Top #1 — ndiddy:

A lot of people here are portraying the opposition to data centers as being uneducated hypocrites who are against anything getting built. When you look at what the opposition are saying, they generally know what they are talking about. Here's Abdul El-Sayed (new Michigan senator) talking about his ideas for regulating the AI industry: https://youtu.be/YX44XDt0gXI?t=182 . For datacenters specifically, he isn't against them being built but thinks that there need to be rules in place so the communities that they're being built in actually benefit from them. He views moratoriums as something that localities and states should be doing until those rules are in place federally. The rules he suggests are:

- There must be community benefits agreements negotiated transparently with the local community

- Any new datacenters being built cannot raise utility rates

- Some of the revenue generated by the datacenter must be set aside to improve power reliability

- Datacenters must not touch our waterways at all

- Datacenters must be built using union labor

A lot of the communities that had datacenters built in them ended up getting steamrolled in negotiations by the tech companies because you had the local government (in small towns, this is people who work part time making a few thousand dollars per year) negotiating a deal with the Google/xAI/Oracle/etc corporate lawyers. I think it makes sense to say that the buildout should be paused until fairer terms can be worked out on a national level, rather than letting this continue to happen.

↳ reply 1 — pj_mukh:

>>“- There must be community benefits agreements negotiated transparently with the local community

- Any new datacenters being built cannot raise utility rates

- Some of the revenue generated by the datacenter must be set aside to improve power reliability

- Datacenters must not touch our waterways at all

- Datacenters must be built using union labor”

Deal. This sounds like a great list. I would add, “no property tax breaks”.

Just get the state to pass this as a law and set appropriate enforcement mechanisms and then just let data centers go ham if they meet this criteria?

No more “per community meetings” and municipal haggling (see: corrupting) local governments. Buy the land build the data centers. The municipality can figure out the exact benefits that works for that community from the giant tax coffers.

This seems imminently fair to me.

↳↳ reply — nomel:

> - Some of the revenue generated by the datacenter must be set aside to improve power reliability

Note that the utility monopolies are posting record profits that have increased steadily over the last decade.

↳↳↳ reply — pj_mukh:

> utility monopolies

This was always a silly idea. You either have health competition or state ownership. Monopolies is literally the worst of both worlds.

↳ reply 2 — sjs382:

> The rules he suggests are

Add effective enforcement with harsh penalties for "ask for forgiveness rather than permission" behavior. We've been on this ride too many times not to know what to expect.

↳ reply 3 — GenerWork:

Florida passed a state law that has standards are somewhat close to what you wrote, yet communities down here still voted to ban datacenter construction.

Top #2 — twiclo:

Kevin Oleary's data center is going to be built one hour from my town. A lot of people here seem upset about it but when I talk to them I can't get a single good reason to oppose the data center. Here's what I hear and my response:

"It'll use too much water." - It's going to use less water than the farm that used to run on this land. The county is gaining water from this.

"Our electrical bills will go up" - They're generating their own electricity and excess power will be put back into the grid

"Noise" - It's an hour away from any structure on a stinky swamp north of the Salt Lake

"Wildlife refuge" - This bird refuge is in Brigham City. The data center will be on the opposite end of the county. Some people seem to think it's right next door.

My concern is I don't want tax payers left holding the bag if this falls apart but it seems like, at least with this DC, that that's not the case. This is going to bring a LOT of money to my county which sorely needs it and a LOT of people to my dying rural town.

I really just have to come to the conclusion that we have a tiktok informed voting block here. I've had people ask me if I'm worried that the new data center will spy on me. What?

Edit: I checked. This is going to use 162 million less gallons per year than the farm.

↳ reply 1 — guitarlimeo:

> They're generating their own electricity and excess power will be put back into the grid

Generating their own electricity how? I would be pissed if I got one of these xAI power turbines near my area [1]. And even if they weren't loud, gas plants are environmentally bad.

> They're generating their own electricity and excess power will be put back into the grid

Electricity prices will go up! The data centers won't keep generate their own electricity if they aren't forced to. They will just take electricity from the grid when it's cheaper than generating, and will start generating only when the costs of generating are lower.

[1] https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/musks-ai-power-plant-ge...

↳↳ reply — twiclo:

They're using natural gas to generate electricity. Everyone involved has said that it won't pull power from the grid. But if it does that's a good thing. That means we'll need to expand our grid. We're currently building a nuclear reactor in my county as well. This is economic growth and a good thing. My town is dying. Main street is depressing. There's a general lack of optimism in the people here.

↳↳↳ reply — tyre:

This is exactly the argument people are worried about. "If prices go up, it's a good thing." For whom? Residents will have to pay this for a decade before a nuclear reactor comes online.

↳ reply 2 — cbg0:

These seem to be very specific to this project, and I doubt the majority of DC projects are like this one, an hour away with its own gas turbines to generate power and plenty of water available.

There also seems to be a Utah-specific bill from last year requiring large electricity users to pay the additional infrastructure and power-supply costs attributable to serving them rather than shifting those costs onto existing utility customers. This is also not the case everywhere DCs are being built.

Top #3 — Dem_Boys:

This comment section blows my mind! Are we that insulated from the world? Are these all bots? Am I crazy???

Tech is now viewed in the same lense as dirty greedy oil companies. If an oil company opened a candy store most people I know would not go because "Oh those oil companies can't be trusted"

Anytime I talk to anyone not in tech they're extremely sceptical of anything tech companies do. Most common reasons I hear as to why is greed, social media destroying children in many ways, seeking political power, and now many parents are concerned their child won't have critical thinking skills because AI is here to think for them.

I don't think they're crazy or obviously wrong. It breaks my heart to hear tech leaders chalk this all up to "AI has poor messaging" as if you say "Our lies have got to be better so we can make the public believe what we want". I've never seen tech so out of touch.

↳ reply 1 — tavavex:

> Tech is now viewed in the same lens as dirty greedy oil companies. If an oil company opened a candy store most people I know would not go because "Oh those oil companies can't be trusted"

That's right, but consider what people would be saying about oil companies on Driller News. Thousands of users here have financial or ideological vested interests in the success of the current crop of tech companies. They can recognize the individual faults of the industry where it doesn't affect their primary interest - such as disliking social media, addictive design and so on - but when you start talking about THE tech golden goose, the criticism dies down.
